Genus and Species Patents and Evergreening

slides.part: Chapter 1: The Protection of Plant Varieties and Farmers’ Rights Act, 2001 (PPVFRA)
slides.title: Why India has a sui generis plant variety law
slides.html:
India protects plant varieties through its own sui generis law, the PPVFRA, adopted in response to Article 27(3)(b) of the TRIPS Agreement.

Bearings on innovation. PPVFRA stands for the Protection of Plant Varieties and Farmers’ Rights Act, 2001. The same initials are also used for the Authority set up under the Act, so read the context to see which is meant.

The Act is India’s sui generis system for plant varieties: a system of protection of its own kind, outside the usual categories of intellectual property. It was India’s response to TRIPS, which leaves members a choice of route.

Article 27(3)(b), TRIPS Agreement. Members may protect plant varieties by patents, by an effective sui generis system, or by both.

India chose the sui generis route. That choice matters: a law of its own kind can be shaped around national needs, and India used the freedom to protect farmers as well as breeders, as the next slide shows.

Remember: TRIPS Article 27(3)(b) offers three doors: patents, sui generis, or both. India took the sui generis door and built the PPVFRA, 2001 behind it.

slides.part: Chapter 1: The Protection of Plant Varieties and Farmers’ Rights Act, 2001 (PPVFRA)
slides.title: Breeders’ rights and farmers’ rights in balance
slides.html:
Unusually, the PPVFRA protects farmers as well as breeders: it balances the incentive to breed new varieties against farmers’ rights and benefit sharing.

Unusually among plant variety laws, the Act protects farmers as well as breeders. Each side receives something different, for a different reason.

FeatureBreedersFarmers
What they getExclusive rights over registered varietiesThe right to save, use, sow, resow, exchange, share or sell farm produce, including seed of a protected variety
The limitThe exclusive rights attach to registered varietiesMay not sell branded seed of a protected variety
Why the law gives itA reason to invest in breedingModern breeding builds on varieties that farming communities conserved and improved over generations

Farmers’ rights and benefit sharing recognise that modern breeding builds on varieties that farming communities conserved and improved over generations. A breeder’s new variety stands on the farmers’ old ones, so the law lets some value flow back to them.

Exam tip: Explain both sides of the balance: the incentive to breed new varieties, and the protection of farmers’ rights and benefit sharing. Do not treat plant variety protection only as an incentive to innovate.

Remember: Farmers keep seven verbs (save, use, sow, resow, exchange, share, sell) but lose one: selling branded seed of a protected variety.

slides.part: Chapter 2: The Biological Diversity Act, 2002 and the CBD
slides.title: The CBD: three objectives and the rules of access
slides.html:
The CBD (Rio, 1992) sets three objectives and makes access to genetic resources subject to national legislation, prior informed consent and mutually agreed terms.

The Convention on Biological Diversity (CBD) was opened for signature at the Rio Earth Summit (United Nations Conference on Environment and Development) in 1992 and entered into force in 1993. It is the parent treaty of the Biological Diversity Act and of the DSI debate in Part B.

Article 1, CBD. Three objectives: (1) conservation of biological diversity; (2) sustainable use of its components; and (3) fair and equitable sharing of the benefits arising out of the utilisation of genetic resources.

In short, the notes say: access, benefit sharing and sustainable use. In an answer, state the three Article 1 objectives in full first and use the shorthand only as a summary.

Article 15, CBD. Recognises the sovereign rights of states over their natural resources and makes access to genetic resources subject to national legislation, prior informed consent (PIC) and mutually agreed terms (MAT).

Article 15 is the root of access and benefit sharing (ABS): a user needs the provider’s consent and agreed terms, and the benefits of use are shared with the provider. The Nagoya Protocol of 2010 develops these ABS obligations (Chapter 4).

slides.part: Chapter 2: The Biological Diversity Act, 2002 and the CBD
slides.title: The Act’s objectives and three levels of authority
slides.html:
The Biological Diversity Act, 2002 implements the CBD in India, mirrors its three objectives and works through national, state and local bodies.

The Biological Diversity Act, 2002 implements the CBD in India. Its objective mirrors the CBD: conservation of biological diversity, sustainable use of its components, and fair and equitable sharing of the benefits arising out of the use of biological resources. It works through three levels of authority.

Table 1: Three level structure under the Biological Diversity Act, 2002. The logic runs from the top down: foreign users answer to the national body, Indian users to the state body, and local communities speak through their own committee.

LevelBodyRole
NationalNational Biodiversity Authority (NBA), ChennaiRegulates access by foreign persons and entities; approves applications for intellectual property rights based on Indian biological resources or associated knowledge; determines benefit sharing. It is India’s competent national authority under the Nagoya Protocol.
StateState Biodiversity Board (SBB)Deals with access by Indian citizens and entities and advises the state government. It may demand fair and equitable benefit sharing from Indian users (Divya Pharmacy).
LocalBiodiversity Management Committee (BMC)Constituted by local bodies (not at district level). Documents local biodiversity in People’s Biodiversity Registers, is consulted on access and may levy fees.

Remember: F-I-L: Foreign users go to the NBA, Indian users to the SBB, and Local bodies set up the BMC.

slides.part: Chapter 2: The Biological Diversity Act, 2002 and the CBD
slides.title: Divya Pharmacy: the dispute
slides.html:
Divya Pharmacy asked whether a State Biodiversity Board can demand benefit sharing from an Indian company, or may only receive prior intimation from it.

Table 2: Case brief: Divya Pharmacy v. Union of India. This is the leading Indian case on benefit sharing by domestic users. Each element is given in detail under the notes’ own headings: this slide covers the dispute, and the next covers the decision.

Divya Pharmacy v. Union of India, 2018 SCC OnLine Utt 1035

Citation
Divya Pharmacy v. Union of India, 2018 SCC OnLine Utt 1035; Writ Petition (M/S) No. 3437 of 2016; High Court of Uttarakhand at Nainital; Sudhanshu Dhulia J.; decided 21 December 2018.
Facts
Divya Pharmacy, a Haridwar based maker of Ayurvedic medicines and nutraceuticals, used herbs from Uttarakhand. The Uttarakhand Biodiversity Board demanded a contribution towards fair and equitable benefit sharing (FEBS) under the 2014 ABS Guidelines. Divya Pharmacy challenged the demand by writ petition.
Issue
Can a State Biodiversity Board demand FEBS from an Indian entity, or does FEBS apply only to foreign entities, with Indian entities bound only to give prior intimation under Section 7?
Arguments
Petitioner: as an Indian entity it had only to intimate the Board, which could restrict harmful activities but could not levy benefit sharing; FEBS under Section 21 is fixed by the NBA when it approves access by foreign entities. Respondents (the Union and the NBA supported the State Board): the Act’s objectives and India’s CBD commitments require benefit sharing by all commercial users.

slides.part: Chapter 2: The Biological Diversity Act, 2002 and the CBD
slides.title: Divya Pharmacy: the purposive reading wins
slides.html:
Reading the Act purposively with the CBD and Nagoya, the High Court held that a State Board may demand benefit sharing from Indian commercial users.

Divya Pharmacy v. Union of India, 2018 SCC OnLine Utt 1035 (continued)

Decision
Writ petition dismissed. The State Biodiversity Board has power to demand FEBS from Divya Pharmacy.
Reasoning
Purposive interpretation. A literal reading favoured the petitioner, but it would produce the anomaly that only foreign users share benefits from Indian resources. The Act was read with the CBD, the Nagoya Protocol and the rights of indigenous and local communities who conserve the resources.
Ratio
FEBS is a regulatory function that a State Biodiversity Board may exercise against an Indian entity using biological resources commercially.
Criticism
Welcomed as an affirmation of community rights; criticised as going beyond the statutory text.

Why did purpose beat text? On the literal reading, an Indian company could use the same herbs from the same forests as a foreign one and share nothing, while the foreign user paid. The court treated that as an anomaly and chose the reading that serves the Act’s objectives and the CBD.

Exam tip: Cite the case as Divya Pharmacy v. Union of India (not “State of Uttarakhand v. Divya Pharmacy”). For the present law, add the 2023 amendment and the 2025 Regulations.

slides.part: Chapter 2: The Biological Diversity Act, 2002 and the CBD
slides.title: The amended framework: 2023 Act, 2024 Rules, 2025 Regulations
slides.html:
Today’s framework rests on three instruments: the 2023 amendment (in force 1 April 2024), the 2024 Rules, and the NBA’s 2025 Regulations replacing the 2014 Guidelines.

  1. The Biological Diversity (Amendment) Act, 2023 received assent on 3 August 2023 and came into force on 1 April 2024.
  2. The Biological Diversity Rules, 2024 were notified on 22 October 2024 and took effect on 22 December 2024.
  3. The NBA notified the Biological Diversity (Access to Biological Resources and Knowledge Associated thereto and Fair and Equitable Sharing of Benefits) Regulations, 2025 in late April 2025, replacing the 2014 Guidelines.

This is why the present law changes how you use Divya Pharmacy: the Board’s demand in that case was made under the 2014 ABS Guidelines, and those Guidelines have now been replaced. Key features of the new framework follow here and on the next slide.

Law update. The 2025 Regulations bring digital sequence information (DSI) within benefit sharing, which the 2014 Guidelines did not. They do not define DSI. DSI itself is explained in Part B (Chapter 3).

slides.part: Chapter 2: The Biological Diversity Act, 2002 and the CBD
slides.title: Benefit sharing amounts, exemptions and the NBA’s share
slides.html:
Under the amended framework, benefit sharing follows turnover, small users are exempt, high value resources pay more, and the NBA’s retained share is criticised.

  1. Turnover link: benefit sharing is linked to annual turnover; users below ₹5 crore are exempt.
  2. High value or threatened resources: higher amounts apply to resources such as red sanders, sandalwood and agarwood (at least 5% of the auction or sale value); in some commercial cases the share can exceed 20%.
  3. Easier routes: the amended framework eases requirements for cultivated medicinal plants and for registered practitioners of Indian systems of medicine (AYUSH).
  4. The NBA’s share: about 10% to 15% of benefit sharing amounts is retained by the NBA, which has been criticised as inconsistent with Section 21(3), which contemplates payment to the benefit claimers.

Read the four together. The law spares the smallest users, eases cultivated and traditional use, and charges most where the resource is scarce or valuable. The criticism of the NBA’s share is textual: Section 21(3) points the money to the benefit claimers, not to the regulator.

Exam tip: Cover three things: the link between the Act and the three CBD objectives; the three level structure (BMCs are set up by local bodies); and Divya Pharmacy with its purposive reasoning, placed in the post 2023 framework.

slides.part: Quick revision
slides.title: Part A at a glance
slides.html:
The PPVFRA balances breeders and farmers; the Biological Diversity Act implements the CBD through the NBA, SBBs and BMCs; Divya Pharmacy extends benefit sharing to Indian users.

  1. PPVFRA, 2001: India’s sui generis plant variety law, adopted in response to TRIPS Article 27(3)(b). Breeders get exclusive rights over registered varieties; farmers may save, use, sow, resow, exchange, share or sell farm produce including seed, but not branded seed of a protected variety.
  2. CBD, 1992 (in force 1993): Article 1 sets three objectives (conservation, sustainable use, fair and equitable benefit sharing); Article 15 makes access subject to national legislation, PIC and MAT.
  3. In India the Biological Diversity Act, 2002 implements the CBD through the NBA, State Boards and BMCs; Divya Pharmacy (2018) held that State Boards may demand benefit sharing from Indian entities; the 2025 Regulations extend benefit sharing to DSI.
  4. Post 2023 framework: amendment in force 1 April 2024; Rules effective 22 December 2024; 2025 Regulations replace the 2014 Guidelines; ₹5 crore turnover exemption; at least 5% for high value resources; NBA retains about 10% to 15%.
BodyDeals withKey powers
NBA (Chennai)Foreign persons and entities; IPR applicationsApproves access and IPRs; determines benefit sharing; Nagoya competent national authority
SBBIndian citizens and entitiesAdvises the state government; may demand FEBS
BMCLocal level (set up by local bodies)People’s Biodiversity Registers; consulted on access; may levy fees

slides.part: Practice questions
slides.title: Practice questions: Part A
slides.html:
1. State the three objectives common to the CBD and the Biological Diversity Act, 2002.
  2. Name the three levels of authority under the Biological Diversity Act and the role of each.
  3. Critically assess Divya Pharmacy v. Union of India and explain how the 2023 amendment affects it.
  4. Explain how the PPVFRA balances the incentive to breed new varieties against farmers’ rights and benefit sharing. (Built from the Chapter 1 exam tip.)

slides.part: Answer plans
slides.title: Answer plans: the objectives and the three levels
slides.html:
Short answers score on precision: name each objective or body exactly, attach its article or role, and close with the point examiners look for.

Q1. State the three objectives common to the CBD and the Biological Diversity Act, 2002.

  1. Open with the CBD: opened for signature at the Rio Earth Summit in 1992, in force in 1993; Article 1 sets the objectives.
  2. State the three objectives in order: conservation of biological diversity; sustainable use of its components; fair and equitable sharing of the benefits arising out of the utilisation of genetic resources.
  3. Show that the Biological Diversity Act, 2002 implements the CBD and mirrors the same objectives (benefits arising out of the use of biological resources).
  4. Add Article 15 (sovereign rights; access subject to national legislation, PIC and MAT) and the Nagoya Protocol, 2010 to show how benefit sharing is put into practice.
  5. Conclude with the notes’ shorthand: access, benefit sharing and sustainable use.

Q2. Name the three levels of authority under the Biological Diversity Act and the role of each.

  1. One line: the Act implements the CBD through three levels of authority. A level, body and role table earns marks.
  2. National: the NBA, Chennai, regulates access by foreign persons and entities, approves IPR applications based on Indian biological resources or associated knowledge, determines benefit sharing, and is India’s competent national authority under Nagoya.
  3. State: the SBB deals with access by Indian citizens and entities, advises the state government and may demand FEBS from Indian users (Divya Pharmacy).
  4. Local: the BMC is constituted by local bodies (not at district level), documents local biodiversity in People’s Biodiversity Registers, is consulted on access and may levy fees.
  5. Conclude by stressing that BMCs are set up by local bodies (the Chapter 2 exam tip).

slides.part: Answer plans
slides.title: Answer plans: Divya Pharmacy and the PPVFRA balance
slides.html:
Analytical answers need a spine: brief the case or law, expose its reasoning, weigh the criticism, then place it in the present framework.

Q3. Critically assess Divya Pharmacy v. Union of India and explain how the 2023 amendment affects it.

  1. Cite correctly: Divya Pharmacy v. Union of India, 2018 SCC OnLine Utt 1035 (Uttarakhand High Court, 2018), not “State of Uttarakhand v. Divya Pharmacy”.
  2. Facts and issue: the Board’s FEBS demand under the 2014 ABS Guidelines; may an SBB demand FEBS from an Indian entity, or only receive prior intimation under Section 7?
  3. Arguments: intimation only, with FEBS under Section 21 fixed by the NBA for foreign access (petitioner), against benefit sharing by all commercial users (respondents).
  4. Holding: petition dismissed. Purposive interpretation avoids the anomaly that only foreign users share benefits, reading the Act with the CBD, Nagoya and community rights. Ratio: FEBS is a regulatory function against Indian commercial users.
  5. Assess: welcomed as affirming community rights; criticised as going beyond the statutory text, which on a literal reading favoured the petitioner.
  6. The 2023 amendment and after: in force 1 April 2024; Rules, 2024; the 2025 Regulations replace the 2014 Guidelines the demand rested on, link benefit sharing to turnover (below ₹5 crore exempt), ease requirements for cultivated medicinal plants and AYUSH practitioners, and include DSI.
  7. Conclude by placing the ratio in the post 2023 framework. The notes do not say the amendment overrules or codifies it, so argue only from these features.

Q4. Explain how the PPVFRA balances the incentive to breed new varieties against farmers’ rights and benefit sharing.

  1. Define: the PPVFRA, 2001, India’s sui generis system under TRIPS Article 27(3)(b) (patents, a sui generis system, or both).
  2. Breeders: exclusive rights over registered varieties give a reason to invest in breeding.
  3. Farmers: may save, use, sow, resow, exchange, share or sell farm produce, including seed of a protected variety, but not branded seed of a protected variety.
  4. Benefit sharing: modern breeding builds on varieties that farming communities conserved and improved over generations.
  5. Conclude: plant variety protection is a balance, not only an incentive to innovate.

slides.part: Chapter 3: Biopiracy, Digital Biopiracy and DSI
slides.title: Biopiracy and digital biopiracy defined
slides.html:
Biopiracy takes biological resources or traditional knowledge without consent or benefit sharing; digital biopiracy does the same with sequence data taken from databases.

Biopiracy
The appropriation of biological resources or associated traditional knowledge, often through patents, without the consent of the provider country or community and without sharing benefits.
Digital biopiracy
Taking digital sequences from gene banks and sequence databases without giving the providers due consideration, that is, without consent, acknowledgment or benefit sharing.
DSI
Digital sequence information.

Both definitions share two missing elements: no consent and no benefit sharing. Digital biopiracy names a third, acknowledgment, because data can be taken without even crediting the provider.

Notice what is being taken. Classic biopiracy concerns a physical resource or knowledge; digital biopiracy concerns information held in databases. That shift drives the rest of Part B: rules built for samples struggle with data.

slides.part: Chapter 3: Biopiracy, Digital Biopiracy and DSI
slides.title: Turmeric, neem and basmati: the Indian response
slides.html:
The classic Indian biopiracy disputes over turmeric, neem and basmati explain why the Patents Act requires disclosure of source and allows opposition on that ground.

Classic Indian examples involved physical resources and traditional knowledge:

  1. Turmeric: the United States patent on the wound healing use of turmeric (No. 5,401,504), revoked in 1997 after a challenge supported by CSIR.
  2. Neem: a European patent on a neem based fungicide, revoked after opposition.
  3. Basmati: the RiceTec patent on basmati lines.

These episodes explain two safeguards in the Patents Act, 1970. The first works at the filing stage; the second lets others fight back.

Section 10(4)(d)(ii)(D), Patents Act, 1970. An applicant must disclose the source and geographical origin of biological material used in an invention.

Section 25(1)(j) and (k), Patents Act, 1970. Opposition lies where that source is not disclosed or wrongly mentioned, or where the invention is anticipated by traditional knowledge.

slides.part: Chapter 3: Biopiracy, Digital Biopiracy and DSI
slides.title: What DSI is: genes written as text
slides.html:
Sequencing turns an organism’s genetic code into text that can be stored, copied, searched and sent, and often turned back into molecules by synthesis.

Every organism carries its genetic information in DNA (some viruses in RNA). Sequencing records the order of the chemical bases as text: a string of the letters A, C, G and T (U in RNA). Protein sequences are written the same way, as strings of amino acid letters.

Once recorded, a sequence can be stored, copied, searched and sent like any other data, and often the corresponding molecule can be made by chemical synthesis without ever handling the source organism.

That is the whole legal problem in miniature: the value of a resource can now travel as data, so rules that watch physical samples see nothing move.

slides.part: Chapter 3: Biopiracy, Digital Biopiracy and DSI
slides.title: The DSI label and where sequence data lives
slides.html:
“DSI” is a placeholder term the CBD has chosen to keep; public sequence data sit mainly in three databases, which are not agricultural gene banks.

The CBD uses “digital sequence information on genetic resources” as a placeholder term. In decision 14/20 the parties noted that it may not be the most appropriate term, and in decision 15/9 they agreed to keep using it. (Recall that India’s 2025 Regulations do not define DSI either.)

Public sequence data sit mainly in GenBank, the European Nucleotide Archive and the DNA Data Bank of Japan, which together form the International Nucleotide Sequence Database Collaboration.

FeatureSequence databaseGene bank (agricultural sense)
What it holdsDigital sequence dataA store of physical seeds or germplasm
ExamplesGenBank, the European Nucleotide Archive, the DNA Data Bank of JapanSeed and germplasm stores
Fit with ABS rulesPoor: ABS rules were not built for dataGood: ABS rules were built for physical material of this kind

Keep the two apart in answers. ABS rules were built for physical material of the gene bank kind, not for data, and that mismatch is the subject of Chapter 4.

slides.part: Chapter 3: Biopiracy, Digital Biopiracy and DSI
slides.title: Why DSI changed the patent game
slides.html:
DSI moves innovation from material to information, so patent and ABS rules designed for a tangible, trackable world struggle to reach it.

  1. From material to information: sequencing turns genetic material into downloadable information, shifting where innovation and legal disputes begin. A sample no longer needs to cross a border for its value to be extracted.
  2. Law has not kept pace: patents, ABS obligations and sovereignty claims were designed for a tangible, trackable world and struggle to map onto digital data.
  3. Consequences for patent law: an invention can be developed from sequence data without the inventor handling the organism, so disclosure duties framed around “biological material” may never be triggered; and because a sequence can be synthesised, there may be no physical sample to follow across a border.

Connect this to Section 10(4)(d)(ii)(D). The duty is to disclose the source of biological material used in an invention. If the inventor only ever worked with a downloaded sequence, the turmeric era safeguard may simply not bite.

Remember: Material becomes information; information crosses no border; with no border crossing, there is no trigger.

slides.part: Chapter 4: The Nagoya Protocol and the DSI Problem
slides.title: The Nagoya Protocol’s three duties
slides.html:
The Nagoya Protocol (adopted 2010, in force 2014) turns CBD access and benefit sharing into provider consent, agreed terms and compliance checks in user countries.

The Nagoya Protocol on Access to Genetic Resources and the Fair and Equitable Sharing of Benefits Arising from their Utilization was adopted in 2010 and entered into force in 2014. It develops the ABS obligations of CBD Article 15.

DutyWhat it requiresWho acts
Prior informed consent (PIC)Consent of the provider country, where its law requires itProvider country
Mutually agreed terms (MAT)Agreed terms on benefit sharingProvider and user
Compliance measuresMeasures in user countries, including checkpoints that monitor utilisationUser country

India is a party, and the NBA is its competent national authority. The design is a chain: consent at the start, a contract in the middle, and checkpoints at the end to catch use that skipped the first two.

Remember: P-M-C: PIC (consent), MAT (contract), Checkpoints (control).

slides.part: Chapter 4: The Nagoya Protocol and the DSI Problem
slides.title: Nagoya was not designed for downloads
slides.html:
Nagoya assumed physical travel, a bilateral contract and a traceable chain of custody; DSI is downloaded from anywhere, with no contract and no PIC.

The Protocol assumed that accessing genetic resources meant physically travelling to a provider country, negotiating a bilateral agreement and signing a contract: a trackable, auditable chain of custody.

DSI can be accessed from anywhere with an internet connection, with no travel, no bilateral contract and no formal PIC, which breaks the transaction logic of ABS at its core. Every ABS duty hangs on a transaction, and with DSI the transaction never happens.

Table 3: Old model and new digital reality.

AspectOld modelNew digital reality
Mode of accessPhysical travelInternet access
Legal basisBilateral agreement, signed contractNo contract, no PIC, immediate download
Point of controlConsent and contract; breach can be tracedNo natural point at which consent is sought or terms agreed

slides.part: Chapter 4: The Nagoya Protocol and the DSI Problem
slides.title: “Who owns the source?” becomes “Who can prove it?”
slides.html:
With DSI the question shifts from ownership to proof: obligations seem to vanish, national rules clash, and providers cannot easily link a product to their sequence.

  1. Obligations appear to vanish: once a sequence enters the public domain, benefit sharing obligations become very hard to enforce in many jurisdictions, and prior access without a contract creates a legal grey zone.
  2. Regulatory patchwork: some states extend national ABS rules expressly to DSI (India does so through the 2025 Regulations) and many do not, producing overlapping and inconsistent compliance demands that create serious risk for international research collaborations.
  3. The evidential problem: a provider must show that a particular product was developed from a particular sequence derived from its resource, and that link is usually invisible once data has been copied between databases.

The three compound one another. A provider such as India may have the law on its side, through the 2025 Regulations, and still fail because it cannot prove the chain from its resource to the product.

Remember: Vanish, Patchwork, Proof: the obligation fades, the rules clash, and the link cannot be shown.

slides.part: Chapter 4: The Nagoya Protocol and the DSI Problem
slides.title: Bilateral assumptions break
slides.html:
PIC and MAT were built for one researcher collecting one sample from one place; DSI bypasses every step, leaving providers strong moral claims but weak legal instruments.

PIC and MAT were designed for a researcher who applied to collect a specific sample from a specific location. DSI bypasses every step of that process.

The “download first” reality undercuts the enforcement pathways of the old model and leaves provider nations with strong moral claims but weak legal instruments.

Table 4: Bilateral assumptions and the DSI reality.

Old bilateral modelDSI reality
PIC requiredNo PIC
Physical sampleDigital download
One to one contractDiffuse sourcing
Enforceable at the borderNo enforcement trigger

Read each row as a lost lever: no consent to withhold, no sample to stop, no single counterparty to hold to a contract, and no border at which to act.

slides.part: Chapter 4: The Nagoya Protocol and the DSI Problem
slides.title: Is data a “genetic resource”?
slides.html:
Read literally, a database sequence is not CBD “material”; providers say value lies in the information, users defend open data, and multilateralism is the compromise.

Genetic resources (CBD)
Genetic material of actual or potential value.
Genetic material (CBD)
Material of plant, animal, microbial or other origin containing functional units of heredity.

On a literal reading, a string of letters in a database is not “material”, so it may fall outside both definitions and outside the ABS duties built on them.

SideArgument
Provider countriesThe value of a resource lies in its information, so benefit sharing should follow the information.
User countries and much of the research communityStress the importance of open databases for science.

The multilateral approach (Chapter 6) is the compromise: data stays open, while commercial users contribute to a common pool.

slides.part: Chapter 5: DSI Governance across UN Forums
slides.title: Four forums, no interoperability
slides.html:
DSI is negotiated in at least four UN instruments at once, without guaranteed interoperability, so the same dataset can face different benefit sharing obligations.

Negotiations on DSI run in parallel in at least four UN instruments without guaranteed interoperability, so the same dataset can face different benefit sharing obligations depending on the forum.

This fragmentation, at the centre of which is “non interoperable DSI data use”, is the central political challenge, not a side effect.

The overall trend is a UN push toward multilateral DSI benefit sharing: away from sample by sample bilateral contracts toward pooled systems, each forum in its own way.

CBD

Biodiversity: the Cali Fund

ITPGRFA

Crops: the Multilateral System

WHO Pandemic Agreement

Pathogens with pandemic potential: the PABS system

BBNJ

Marine organisms of the high seas

Remember: One dataset, four doors: Biodiversity (CBD), Crops (ITPGRFA), Pathogens (WHO), Marine (BBNJ).

slides.part: Chapter 5: DSI Governance across UN Forums
slides.title: The CBD and the ITPGRFA on DSI
slides.html:
The CBD runs a fund with indicative contribution rates; the ITPGRFA gives facilitated access to listed crops with mandatory payment in defined cases.

Table 5: The four UN forums on DSI (first two forums).

ForumApproach to DSIKey points for the exam
CBDMultilateral mechanism with a global fund, the Cali Fund (decision 16/2, 2024). DSI stays openly accessible; large users are expected to contribute 1% of profits or 0.1% of revenue.A move away from the bilateral PIC and MAT model. National laws (such as India’s 2025 Regulations) may still impose their own requirements.
ITPGRFA (International Treaty on Plant Genetic Resources for Food and Agriculture)Multilateral System of facilitated access to listed food and forage crops under a standard material transfer agreement, with a payment to a benefit sharing fund when a commercialised product is not available without restriction for further research and breeding.Free access, with mandatory payment in defined cases. Coverage of DSI is still under negotiation.

Spot the shared idea and the difference. Both pool benefits instead of bargaining sample by sample. But under the CBD large users are expected to contribute at indicative rates, while under the ITPGRFA payment is mandatory in a defined case.

slides.part: Chapter 5: DSI Governance across UN Forums
slides.title: The WHO Pandemic Agreement and BBNJ
slides.html:
The WHO system shares a slice of production, not money; BBNJ tracks high seas marine DSI and shares money afterwards through a fund.

Table 5: The four UN forums on DSI (continued).

ForumApproach to DSIKey points for the exam
WHO Pandemic Agreement (negotiated as “WHO CA+”)Pathogen Access and Benefit Sharing (PABS) system, Article 12: participating manufacturers give WHO rapid access to 20% of their real time production of vaccines, therapeutics and diagnostics in a pandemic emergency, at least 10% as a donation and the rest at affordable prices.The 20% is a share of production, not a money payment. The Agreement was adopted in May 2025, but the PABS annex was not ready by May 2026 and negotiations continue; the Agreement opens for signature only after the annex is adopted.
BBNJ (Agreement on marine biological diversity of areas beyond national jurisdiction)Covers marine genetic resources and DSI on them from the high seas; requires notification through a clearing house mechanism with standardised identifiers (tracking); monetary benefit sharing through a fund.Free access with extensive tracking and benefit payments after the event. Entered into force in January 2026.

Law update. As the notes stand (law stated as on 9 November 2026), the PABS annex is still being negotiated, so the WHO Agreement is not yet open for signature; BBNJ has been in force since January 2026.

Why it matters: a genomic dataset containing plant, microbial and viral sequences might be relevant to the CBD (biodiversity), the ITPGRFA (crops), the WHO system (pathogens with pandemic potential) and BBNJ (marine organisms). A company could face overlapping contribution expectations, or none, depending on how each regime defines its scope.

slides.part: Chapter 6: The COP16 Decision, the Cali Fund and the Policy Choices
slides.title: COP16 and the birth of the Cali Fund
slides.html:
At COP16 in Cali (2024), decision 16/2 adopted a multilateral benefit sharing mechanism for DSI, with a global fund named the Cali Fund.

At COP16 (Cali, Colombia, 2024) the CBD formally adopted the modalities for operationalising a multilateral benefit sharing mechanism for DSI (decision 16/2), a shift from years of negotiation to a concrete policy structure.

It includes a global fund to secure fair and equitable benefit sharing, moving away from the bilateral, per sample model that DSI had made unworkable (Chapter 4).

The Cali Fund for the Fair and Equitable Sharing of Benefits from the Use of DSI is named after the host city. It signals that the debate has moved from whether to share benefits to how to do it at scale. The Fund opened for contributions in February 2025.

Remember: Cali: COP16, decision 16/2, 2024; the Fund opened in February 2025.

slides.part: Chapter 6: The COP16 Decision, the Cali Fund and the Policy Choices
slides.title: What the COP decision requires
slides.html:
The COP decision asks parties to implement the agreed modalities at once, keep working on further options, and sustain the political will to turn decisions into law.

  1. Implement modalities: parties must begin at once to implement the agreed benefit sharing modalities under the multilateral framework.
  2. Explore further options: the CBD directs continued work on additional modalities, acknowledging that the first step is not the last.
  3. Sustain momentum: political will must survive election cycles and changes of government so that COP decisions become durable domestic law.

The third point explains why the first two matter. The aim, in the notes’ words, is that COP decisions become durable domestic law, and that needs political will that outlasts any one government.

Remember: I-E-S: Implement now, Explore more, Sustain the will.

slides.part: Chapter 6: The COP16 Decision, the Cali Fund and the Policy Choices
slides.title: Traceability and databases
slides.html:
A DSI fund needs traceability to work, and the databases where sequences are stored and labelled have become the new battleground of ABS law.

Traceability is the linchpin. The mechanism needs traceability logic, not only good intentions: a fund without a provenance trail is equity without accountability. Without knowing what data was used, by whom and at what commercial scale, contributions cannot be fairly assessed or collected.

Databases become the battleground. The CBD is exploring “possible new tools and models, such as databases” to make DSI publicly available in transparent and accountable ways. How data is stored, labelled and accessed is now a policy question.

Benefit sharing depends on database governance:

  1. who runs the database;
  2. under what rules;
  3. with what metadata.

These are the new frontlines of ABS law. In the physical world the checkpoint was the border; in the digital world it is the database.

slides.part: Chapter 6: The COP16 Decision, the Cali Fund and the Policy Choices
slides.title: Harmonisation and the measurement problem
slides.html:
Scientists urge harmonised DSI rules across all UN frameworks, but three obstacles stand in the way: ABS compatibility, speed of reuse and attribution at scale.

Harmonisation is now an emergency. Scientists writing in Nature Communications have argued that DSI benefit sharing rules must be harmonised across all UN frameworks to preserve the open access principles of global science. The goal is both openness and equity: database interoperability together with better benefit sharing outcomes for provider countries.

  1. ABS compatibility: any solution must stay compatible with the Nagoya Protocol’s existing obligations, which were not designed for digital data.
  2. Speed of reuse: DSI can be downloaded, reanalysed and built into a commercial product faster than regulation can update, so measuring benefits in real time is effectively impossible with current tools.
  3. Attribution at scale: when one genome database holds millions of sequences from hundreds of countries, attributing commercial value to any single sequence becomes statistically and legally intractable.

Remember: A-S-A: ABS compatibility, Speed of reuse, Attribution at scale. The measurement problem is the political problem.

slides.part: Chapter 6: The COP16 Decision, the Cali Fund and the Policy Choices
slides.title: Five policy options, each with friction
slides.html:
There are five ways to share DSI benefits, from bilateral deals to capacity development; decision 16/2 chose the multilateral fund, and each option creates friction with another.

Table 6: Policy options for DSI benefit sharing; each creates friction with another.

OptionHow it worksComment
1. Bilateral transactionalCase by case agreements tied to each DSI access event.Closest to the Nagoya model; hard to apply to downloads.
2. Multilateral fund basedPooled contributions distributed by a central governance body.The model chosen in decision 16/2 (Cali Fund).
3. Subscription feesUsers pay ongoing access fees tied to commercial activity.Would require changing the free access policies of public databases.
4. Levies on productsA percentage of revenue from DSI derived products funds the mechanism.Close to the Cali Fund’s indicative rates.
5. Capacity developmentNon monetary benefits: training, technology transfer, joint research.Usually combined with monetary options.

Read the comments as trade-offs. Option 1 fits Nagoya but not downloads; option 3 would end free database access; option 5 rarely stands alone. The Cali Fund is option 2, with rates that resemble option 4.

slides.part: Chapter 6: The COP16 Decision, the Cali Fund and the Policy Choices
slides.title: The open access multilateral route
slides.html:
Multilateral regimes keep data open but route revenue from commercial use to a fund; providers trade sovereignty for predictability, while patents outrun benefit sharing.

Multilateral regimes regulate commercial use of DSI and route the revenue to a global or regional fund. Country of origin tags are not required for every sequence, but openness is bounded by regime obligations.

The trade off: provider states give up direct bilateral control and gain access to a reliable, collectively funded pool. Sovereignty is traded for predictability, a compromise not all nations accept easily.

Provider statesUnder the multilateral route
Give upDirect bilateral control
GainAccess to a reliable, collectively funded pool
Net effectSovereignty traded for predictability

Patents accelerate, traceability slows. Innovation cycles in genomics and artificial intelligence are shortening and patent filings move at market speed, while benefit sharing frameworks move at the pace of multilateral diplomacy. The gap between the two speeds is where equity is lost.

slides.part: Chapter 6: The COP16 Decision, the Cali Fund and the Policy Choices
slides.title: The Cali Fund’s design logic
slides.html:
Rather than trace each sequence, which is impossible at scale, the Cali Fund aggregates revenue from DSI products and targets commercialisation, not research.

  1. Born from COP16 consensus: a multilateral financial vehicle for biodiversity, the first to treat DSI expressly as a source of commercial value that calls for equitable benefit sharing.
  2. Bypassing the impossible: instead of tracking the origin of each sequence, which is logistically impossible at scale, the Fund looks to aggregate revenue from products that use DSI.
  3. A focus on outcomes: it targets commercialisation, not research, which broadens the contribution base while protecting scientific openness.

The second point is the answer to the attribution problem of 6.4: if no one can say which sequence produced which profit, the Fund stops asking and looks at the products instead. The third keeps databases open, because research use is not what the Fund targets.

slides.part: Chapter 6: The COP16 Decision, the Cali Fund and the Policy Choices
slides.title: The Cali Fund step by step
slides.html:
Figure 1: Operation of the Cali Fund: data stays open, large users pay at indicative rates, money is pooled and allocated, and contributors receive a certificate.

  1. DSI on genetic resources is deposited in public databases and remains openly accessible.
  2. Researchers and companies use DSI; the multilateral mechanism itself requires no case by case PIC or MAT (national law may still apply).
  3. Large users in sectors that benefit from DSI contribute at indicative rates of 1% of profits or 0.1% of revenue.
  4. Contributions are pooled in the Cali Fund.
  5. Funds are allocated to support the CBD objectives, with at least half meant for the needs of indigenous peoples and local communities.
  6. Contributors paying at the indicative rates receive a Cali Fund certificate for that year.

Note the bracket in step 2: national law may still apply. That is how India can keep its own DSI rules alongside the Fund (6.9).

slides.part: Chapter 6: The COP16 Decision, the Cali Fund and the Policy Choices
slides.title: COP17 in Yerevan: the latest position
slides.html:
COP17 (Yerevan, October 2026) set up a working group and an allocation expert group, tied certificates to the indicative rates, and showed how little has been paid.

Law update. Latest position: COP17 (Yerevan, 19 to 30 October 2026). Law stated as on 9 November 2026.

  1. A working group on benefit sharing from DSI was set up, subject to available resources, to develop the mechanism and the Cali Fund further and report to COP18.
  2. Only monetary contributions in line with the indicative rates (1% of profit or 0.1% of revenue) entitle a user to a Cali Fund certificate for the year.
  3. Parties hosting sequence databases were addressed, and parties with users in their jurisdiction were invited to take measures encouraging contributions.
  4. On allocation, an expert group on the allocation methodology was set up; disbursement is planned after COP18, with payments on an exceptional basis if contributions reach USD 150 million.
  5. Contributions remain tiny: only about USD 10,000 had been pledged by the end of COP17, against an aim of about USD 1 billion a year. No large company from the main DSI using sectors had contributed.

The gap between USD 10,000 and USD 1 billion is the best evidence for the critical analysis in 6.10.

slides.part: Chapter 6: The COP16 Decision, the Cali Fund and the Policy Choices
slides.title: India’s dual track on DSI
slides.html:
India runs a national DSI benefit sharing rule (the 2025 Regulations) while supporting the multilateral mechanism; how the two fit for the same use is unsettled.

India combines a national ABS requirement for DSI (the 2025 Regulations, made in light of the COP16 decision) with support for the multilateral mechanism.

TrackInstrumentWhat it asks
NationalBiological Diversity Act, 2002 as amended in 2023, and the 2025 Regulations (DSI included)Benefit sharing under Indian law
MultilateralCBD decision 16/2 and the Cali FundContributions from large users at indicative rates

How the two interact for the same use is not yet settled, for example where a company contributes to the Cali Fund and also owes benefit sharing under Indian law. The notes leave the question open, and so should your answer: identify the overlap as an unresolved issue.

This links back to the regulatory patchwork of 4.3: India is one of the states that extend national ABS rules expressly to DSI.

slides.part: Chapter 6: The COP16 Decision, the Cali Fund and the Policy Choices
slides.title: Critical analysis: workable but voluntary
slides.html:
The Cali Fund solves attribution by abandoning it: workable, but voluntary in practice, and its likely next step would revive open science concerns.

The Cali Fund solves the attribution problem by abandoning attribution: contributions are tied to a user’s overall profit or revenue, not to particular sequences.

That makes it workable but voluntary in practice, and the contribution record shows the weakness of a mechanism without a legal duty to pay.

The emphasis on traceability and database governance points to the likely next step: linking database access or certificates to contribution. That would raise the open science concerns the multilateral route was meant to avoid.

Strength

Workable: no need to trace each sequence

Weakness

Voluntary in practice: no legal duty to pay, and tiny contributions

Likely next step

Link database access or certificates to contribution

Risk

Open science concerns return

slides.part: Quick revision
slides.title: Part B at a glance
slides.html:
Biopiracy has gone digital; Nagoya’s sample and contract model cannot catch downloads; the UN response is multilateral, led by the Cali Fund, but not yet interoperable.

  1. Biopiracy is the unconsented and uncompensated appropriation of biological resources or traditional knowledge; digital biopiracy does the same with sequence data.
  2. The Nagoya model of PIC, MAT and checkpoints assumes a physical sample and a contract, and DSI bypasses both.
  3. The UN response is multilateral: the CBD’s Cali Fund (decision 16/2, refined at COP17 in October 2026), the WHO PABS system (annex still under negotiation), the ITPGRFA and BBNJ, which are not yet interoperable.
  4. India: the 2025 Regulations extend benefit sharing to DSI, alongside support for the multilateral mechanism; how the two interact is not yet settled.
  5. The Cali Fund abandons attribution (contributions follow overall profit or revenue): workable but voluntary in practice.

slides.part: Practice questions
slides.title: Practice questions: Part B
slides.html:
1. Define biopiracy and digital biopiracy. Why does DSI make biopiracy harder to prove?
  2. What is the Cali Fund, and how are contributions calculated?
  3. What does the 20% figure in Article 12 of the WHO Pandemic Agreement refer to?
  4. “The Nagoya Protocol was not designed for downloads.” Discuss with reference to PIC, MAT and enforcement.
  5. Is the open access multilateral route a fair compromise for provider countries? Discuss the trade between sovereignty and predictability.
  6. Problem: A European biotechnology company downloads sequence data of a soil microbe collected in Uttarakhand from a public database, designs an enzyme from it and patents the enzyme in India and Europe. No Indian authority was approached. Advise the National Biodiversity Authority.

slides.part: Answer plans
slides.title: Answer plans: biopiracy and the Cali Fund
slides.html:
For short answers: define precisely, give the figure or provision, then add one sentence on why it matters.

Q1. Define biopiracy and digital biopiracy. Why does DSI make biopiracy harder to prove?

  1. Define biopiracy (appropriation of biological resources or associated traditional knowledge, often through patents, without consent of the provider country or community and without benefit sharing) and digital biopiracy (taking digital sequences from gene banks and sequence databases without consent, acknowledgment or benefit sharing).
  2. Give the classic examples (turmeric patent No. 5,401,504, revoked in 1997; neem; RiceTec basmati) and India’s response in Sections 10(4)(d)(ii)(D) and 25(1)(j) and (k) of the Patents Act, 1970.
  3. Explain DSI: sequences as text that can be stored, copied, searched and sent; molecules synthesised without the organism.
  4. Why harder to prove: the evidential problem (a particular product must be linked to a particular sequence, a link usually invisible once data is copied between databases); no physical sample to follow across a border; disclosure duties framed around “biological material” may never be triggered.
  5. Conclude: “Who owns the source?” becomes “Who can prove it?”

Q2. What is the Cali Fund, and how are contributions calculated?

  1. Define: the global fund created by CBD decision 16/2 at COP16 (Cali, Colombia, 2024), named after the host city; opened for contributions in February 2025.
  2. Calculation: large users in sectors that benefit from DSI contribute at indicative rates of 1% of profits or 0.1% of revenue, tied to overall profit or revenue, not to particular sequences.
  3. Operation: DSI stays openly accessible; no case by case PIC or MAT under the mechanism; contributions pooled; at least half for indigenous peoples and local communities; a certificate for those who pay at the indicative rates.
  4. Latest (COP17): only monetary contributions at the indicative rates earn a certificate; about USD 10,000 pledged against an aim of about USD 1 billion a year.
  5. Conclude: workable but voluntary in practice.

slides.part: Answer plans
slides.title: Answer plans: the WHO 20% and Nagoya’s limits
slides.html:
Fix the figure precisely, then for the essay set out the Nagoya model and show exactly where DSI breaks it.

Q3. What does the 20% figure in Article 12 of the WHO Pandemic Agreement refer to?

  1. Identify: the WHO Pandemic Agreement (negotiated as “WHO CA+”), Article 12, the PABS system.
  2. State: participating manufacturers give WHO rapid access to 20% of their real time production of vaccines, therapeutics and diagnostics in a pandemic emergency, at least 10% as a donation and the rest at affordable prices.
  3. Stress that the 20% is a share of production, not a money payment, unlike the Cali Fund’s 1% or 0.1%.
  4. Status: adopted in May 2025; the PABS annex was not ready by May 2026; the Agreement opens for signature only after the annex is adopted.

Q4. “The Nagoya Protocol was not designed for downloads.” Discuss with reference to PIC, MAT and enforcement.

  1. Introduce Nagoya: adopted 2010, in force 2014; PIC of the provider country, MAT on benefit sharing, compliance measures and checkpoints in user countries; India is a party and the NBA its competent national authority.
  2. The assumption: physical travel, a bilateral agreement and a signed contract, giving a trackable, auditable chain of custody.
  3. PIC: designed for a researcher collecting a specific sample from a specific location; DSI is downloaded with no formal PIC (Tables 3 and 4).
  4. MAT: the one to one contract gives way to diffuse sourcing, with no contract at all.
  5. Enforcement: no enforcement trigger at the border; obligations appear to vanish once a sequence is in the public domain; regulatory patchwork; the evidential problem.
  6. Is data even a “genetic resource”? The CBD definitions of genetic resources and genetic material; the literal reading against the providers’ argument.
  7. Conclude: providers have strong moral claims but weak legal instruments; the response is the multilateral mechanism (decision 16/2), which must stay compatible with Nagoya.

slides.part: Answer plans
slides.title: Answer plan: is the multilateral route fair?
slides.html:
An evaluative essay: define the route, give the case for and against, test it against the alternatives and India’s position, then commit to a reasoned view.

Q5. Is the open access multilateral route a fair compromise for provider countries? Discuss the trade between sovereignty and predictability.

  1. Define the route: multilateral regimes regulate commercial use of DSI and route revenue to a global or regional fund; country of origin tags are not required for every sequence; openness is bounded by regime obligations.
  2. Why it was needed: the bilateral, per sample model is unworkable for DSI; attribution at scale is intractable; reuse outpaces regulation.
  3. For: a reliable, collectively funded pool; at least half for indigenous peoples and local communities; scientific openness protected by targeting commercialisation, not research; the debate moves from whether to how.
  4. Against: sovereignty is traded for predictability, which not all nations accept; voluntary in practice (about USD 10,000 pledged against about USD 1 billion a year; no large company contributed); patents accelerate while traceability slows, and the gap is where equity is lost.
  5. Alternatives (Table 6): bilateral, subscription fees, levies and capacity development, each creating friction with another.
  6. India’s dual track: national 2025 Regulations alongside multilateral support, with the interaction unsettled.
  7. Conclude with a reasoned view, for example fair in design but not yet in delivery; note that the likely next step (linking database access or certificates to contribution) would revive open science concerns.

slides.part: Answer plans
slides.title: Answer plan: the Uttarakhand soil microbe problem
slides.html:
Follow the notes’ structure (Issues, Rules, Application, Conclusion) and keep the national, bilateral and multilateral routes apart.

Q6. Problem: A European biotechnology company downloads sequence data of a soil microbe collected in Uttarakhand from a public database, designs an enzyme from it and patents the enzyme in India and Europe. No Indian authority was approached. Advise the National Biodiversity Authority.

  1. Issues: whether use of DSI is access or utilisation requiring approval or benefit sharing under Indian law; whether the Indian patent application needed NBA approval or disclosure of source; what can be done about the European patent.
  2. Rules: Biological Diversity Act, 2002 as amended in 2023 and the 2025 Regulations (DSI included); Patents Act, 1970, Sections 10(4)(d)(ii)(D) and 25(1)(j); CBD and Nagoya Protocol (bilateral baseline); decision 16/2 and the Cali Fund (multilateral contribution).
  3. Application: the 2025 Regulations bring DSI within benefit sharing, but enforcement against a foreign user with no presence in India depends on jurisdiction and on checkpoints in the user country. In India, non disclosure of source can found an opposition or revocation challenge. Abroad, the NBA must rely on that country’s compliance measures and on the expectation of a Cali Fund contribution.
  4. Strengthen the application with points from the slides: the NBA approves applications for IPRs based on Indian biological resources or associated knowledge; the 2025 Regulations do not define DSI; and the evidential problem of linking the enzyme to the Uttarakhand sequence.
  5. Conclusion: a strong claim in principle with limited practical enforcement; oppose the Indian application, use Nagoya compliance channels, and press for a Cali Fund contribution.

slides.part: Chapter 8: Terms and Legal Frameworks
slides.title: Genus and species patents
slides.html:
A genus patent claims a whole family of compounds; a species patent later claims one member of it. Part C asks whether that second patent is a real invention.

Genus patent
A broad structural claim, often drafted as a Markush group, covering a large class of chemical compounds that share a common scaffold. Such claims are deliberately wide and can capture thousands of possible molecules in one filing.
Species patent
A later, specific claim to one compound within the genus, often the most pharmacologically active one, filed after clinical data confirms its superior efficacy.

The central legal question: is a species patent a genuine invention, or merely an obvious extension of the genus? Courts in several jurisdictions have answered with growing scepticism toward strategic pharmaceutical filings.

Why the order of filing matters: the genus comes first and wide, the species later and narrow. If the species patent stands, protection for that one drug runs on after the genus patent ends. That is why Chapter 9 treats the practice as evergreening.

The real genus and species pairs you will meet in Chapter 10:

Drug (case)Genus (earlier)Species (later)
Linagliptin (Boehringer)IN ’719, since expiredSpecies patent covering linagliptin
Risdiplam (Roche v. Natco)WO ’916 and US ’955, whose Markush formula covered itIN 334397
Semaglutide (Novo Nordisk)IN 275964, filed in 2003, since expiredIN 262697, priority date 18 March 2005

slides.part: Chapter 8: Terms and Legal Frameworks
slides.title: Markush claims: one formula, millions of compounds
slides.html:
A Markush claim describes a core scaffold and lists the permitted groups at each variable position, so one formula claims every combination: millions, even billions, of compounds.

A small molecule drug has a core structure (the scaffold) to which different atoms or groups can be attached at defined positions. A Markush claim describes the scaffold and lists, for each variable position (R1, R2 and so on), the permitted substituents.

Because every combination is claimed, one formula can cover millions or even billions of compounds, though the specification usually describes and tests only a few. That gap, between what is claimed and what is actually shown, drives every dispute in this Part.

The format is named after Eugene Markush, whose United States patent of the 1920s used it.

Exam focus. Keep the two questions in the illustration apart. “Already disclosed” is a novelty attack (Section 64(1)(e)); “made obvious” is an inventive step attack (Section 64(1)(f)). In the risdiplam case the two benches divided on exactly this line (Chapter 10).

slides.part: Chapter 8: Terms and Legal Frameworks
slides.title: Three regimes: novelty versus disclosure
slides.html:
The United States, India and Europe each police broad genus claims and later species claims differently: through enablement, through Section 3(d), and through sufficiency of disclosure.

RegimeApproachNote
United States: 35 U.S.C. § 112Enablement and written description. A genus claim must enable its full scope: a person skilled in the art must be able to make and use the whole claimed genus without undue experimentation.Leading authority: Amgen v. Sanofi (2023). Obviousness is separate, under § 103.
India: Section 3(d), Patents Act, 1970The most aggressive anti evergreening provision globally. New forms of known substances (salts, polymorphs, isomers and others) are not patentable unless they show significantly enhanced efficacy.Interpreted in Novartis (2013). Validity challenges also use Section 64(1)(a), (e) and (f), raised as a defence under Section 107.
Europe: Article 83 EPCDisclosure must be “clear and complete” enough for a person skilled in the art to carry out the invention. A broad genus claim must be matched by an enabling disclosure of its full scope.The European Patent Convention is a separate treaty administered by the European Patent Office; it is not EU law. Inventive step: Article 56 EPC.

Table 7: Three regimes on the genus and species problem

Read the rows as three answers to one problem: a genus claims more than it shows. The United States and Europe ask whether the disclosure is wide enough to support the claim. India adds a filter aimed at the later patent, since a new form must prove enhanced efficacy, and any later patent can still be attacked as not new or obvious.

Caveat. The EPC is not EU law. Calling it European Union law is one of the common mistakes listed for Part C.

slides.part: Chapter 8: Terms and Legal Frameworks
slides.title: Indian provisions used in these disputes
slides.html:
Indian genus and species disputes run on one toolkit: the definition of invention, Section 3(d), three revocation grounds in Section 64(1), and Section 107, which makes them defences.

ProvisionContentRole in genus and species cases
Section 2(1)(j) and (ja)Definitions of “invention” (new product or process involving an inventive step and capable of industrial application) and “inventive step”.Basis of novelty and non obviousness.
Section 3(d)A new form of a known substance that does not enhance its known efficacy is not an invention. The Explanation treats salts, esters, polymorphs, isomers and other derivatives as the same substance unless they differ significantly in properties with regard to efficacy.Used against species patents on derivatives of a known compound (Novartis; Boehringer).
Section 64(1)(a)Revocation where the invention was claimed in a valid claim of earlier priority date in another Indian patent (prior claiming).Requires identity of claims (Novo Nordisk, Division Bench).
Section 64(1)(e)Revocation where the invention is not new, having regard to what was publicly known, used or published before the priority date.Anticipation by the genus patent’s disclosure; the coverage versus disclosure debate.
