Table 8: Provisions of the Patents Act, 1970 used in genus and species disputes

Remember: the three revocation grounds as a, e, f: Already claimed (prior claiming), Earlier known (not new), Foreseeable (obvious). Section 107 turns each into a defence.

Exam focus. Section 64(1)(a) is prior claiming, not anticipation by disclosure; anticipation is Section 64(1)(e). Mixing them up is a listed common mistake.

slides.part: Chapter 9: Evergreening
slides.title: What evergreening is and why it matters
slides.html:
Evergreening stretches a drug monopoly beyond the standard 20 year term through successive, slightly modified patents: legal in design, but increasingly challenged as an abuse.

Evergreening is the pharmaceutical industry’s strategic practice of extending patent monopolies beyond the standard 20 year term through successive, incrementally modified patents. It is legal in design but increasingly challenged as an abuse of the patent system.

The stakes are high. It is said to cost public health systems billions annually, and it has been criticised by the WHO, MSF and UN Special Rapporteurs as a barrier to access to essential medicines.

Three features explain how it works and whom it hurts:

Strategic withholding

Species data is deliberately held back when the genus is filed, enabling a separate, later species application and effectively doubling the period of exclusivity.

The double patenting trap

Overlapping claims on the same inventive concept are filed in several applications, staggered in time to maintain market exclusivity.

The human cost

Delayed generic entry means delayed access to affordable, life saving medicines, which falls hardest on low income countries.

Exam focus. Tie each feature to a case: strategic withholding to Novo Nordisk (semaglutide, “invented in 2004”); serial filings on one inventive concept to Boehringer (linagliptin).

slides.part: Chapter 9: Evergreening
slides.title: Indian tools against evergreening
slides.html:
India can resist evergreening at every stage of a patent’s life: at examination, through opposition, through revocation or a defence in court, and through compulsory licensing.

Indian tools against evergreening, in the order a patent meets them:

  1. Examination: Section 3(d) keeps out new forms of known substances that do not enhance known efficacy.
  2. Opposition: pre grant and post grant opposition under Section 25.
  3. Litigation: revocation under Section 64, and the Section 107 defence in infringement suits.
  4. After grant: compulsory licensing under Section 84 onwards.

The cases in Chapter 10 show courts using the revocation grounds at the interim injunction stage. The pattern repeats: the patentee sues a generic maker and seeks an interim injunction, and the generic maker answers with a credible challenge to validity under Section 107 read with Section 64. If the challenge is credible, the injunction is refused and the generic maker can carry on while the suit goes to trial.

Exam focus. A credible challenge is a serious and substantial question on validity, enough to refuse an injunction without deciding validity. Never write that a species patent was “held invalid” in an interim decision.

slides.part: Chapter 10: Case Briefs
slides.title: Novartis: therapeutic efficacy under Section 3(d)
slides.html:
Novartis (2013) is the foundational blow: a new form of a known medicine passes Section 3(d) only with significantly enhanced therapeutic efficacy, and better bioavailability alone is not enough.

Novartis AG v. Union of India, (2013) 6 SCC 1

Citation
Novartis AG v. Union of India, (2013) 6 SCC 1; Supreme Court of India; decided 1 April 2013; Aftab Alam and Ranjana Prakash Desai JJ.
Facts
Novartis sought a patent for the beta crystalline form of imatinib mesylate (Glivec or Gleevec), a breakthrough cancer drug. The compound was already known; Novartis claimed a specific polymorph with 30% greater bioavailability.
Issues
Whether the beta crystalline form was an “invention” (new and inventive), and whether Section 3(d) excluded it as a new form of a known substance without enhanced efficacy.
Reasoning
Section 3(d) requires significantly enhanced therapeutic efficacy, not merely better bioavailability or physicochemical properties such as stability or flow. Increased bioavailability counts only if shown to produce enhanced therapeutic efficacy. The Court also held imatinib mesylate already disclosed in an earlier patent, and disapproved of a patent law in which there is a wide gap between what a patent covers and what it discloses.
Judgment
The Court unanimously rejected the patent application; appeal dismissed.
Key point
Derivatives of a known substance are treated as the same substance unless they differ significantly in properties with regard to efficacy; for medicines, efficacy means therapeutic efficacy.
Global impact
A template for countries balancing TRIPS obligations with public health; it confirmed India’s right to keep a high patentability bar within the WTO framework.

Table 9: Case brief: Novartis AG v. Union of India

Exam focus. The 30% figure is bioavailability, not therapeutic efficacy, which is exactly why the claim failed. Note also the Court’s warning about the gap between what a patent covers and what it discloses: Chapter 11 builds on it.

slides.part: Chapter 10: Case Briefs
slides.title: Boehringer: the linagliptin facts
slides.html:
Boehringer (2023) is the serial filing case: a genus patent and a later linagliptin species patent, asserted against six Indian manufacturers who challenged the species patent’s validity.

Boehringer Ingelheim v. Vee Excel Drugs, 2023:DHC:2249

Citation
Boehringer Ingelheim Pharma GmbH and Co. KG v. Vee Excel Drugs and Pharmaceuticals Pvt. Ltd. and connected matters, CS(COMM) 239/2019; Delhi High Court; Amit Bansal J.; decided 29 March 2023; 2023:DHC:2249.
Facts
Boehringer held an earlier genus patent (IN ’719, since expired) and a later species patent covering linagliptin, a DPP 4 inhibitor for type 2 diabetes, filed at staggered intervals. It sued six Indian manufacturers, including Vee Excel, Alkem, Micro Labs, Natco and Mankind, for infringing the species patent. In two 2019 suits it had also alleged infringement of the genus patent. Ad interim injunctions had been granted in May 2019. The defendants challenged validity and stressed that their linagliptin was far cheaper.
Issues
(1) Did the defendants raise a credible challenge to the species patent, in particular was linagliptin disclosed or claimed in the genus patent? (2) Was the species patent an impermissible extension of the monopoly, including under Section 3(d)? (3) Should an interim injunction issue, given balance of convenience and public interest?

Table 10: Case brief: Boehringer Ingelheim v. Vee Excel Drugs

One detail in the facts decides the case: in 2019 Boehringer sued on its genus patent as well as the species patent. To say that linagliptin infringed the genus, it had to say that the genus reached linagliptin. The next slide shows what that cost it.

slides.part: Chapter 10: Case Briefs
slides.title: Boehringer: one patent for one inventive concept
slides.html:
Having sued on its genus patent, Boehringer could not deny that the genus disclosed linagliptin, so the species patent was prima facie vulnerable and no injunction issued.

Boehringer Ingelheim v. Vee Excel Drugs (2023): reasoning and result

Reasoning
  1. Following AstraZeneca v. Intas (Division Bench, 2021): once a patentee asserts that its genus patent covers a product, it cannot deny that the product was disclosed there.
  2. Boehringer could not have sued on the genus patent in 2019 unless linagliptin was disclosed or claimed in it. The species patent was therefore prima facie vulnerable, including on prior claiming.
  3. Under Section 3(d), no enhanced efficacy of linagliptin over the genus was shown (Novartis).
  4. The Court examined, with reference to Bishwanath Prasad Radhey Shyam v. Hindustan Metal Industries, whether an older patent should be presumed valid at the interim stage, and noted that observations of the Himachal Pradesh High Court in related litigation were at variance with its findings.
  5. Filing multiple patents for the same inventive concept in series is impermissible: one patent for one inventive concept.
Judgment
Interim injunction refused; earlier ad interim injunctions vacated; the defendants were free to make and sell linagliptin.
Doctrinal shift
The true test is the inventive concept, not the formal structure of the claim. The patent term cannot be extended through later species filings, which raises the bar for species patent holders seeking injunctions against generics.

Exam tip. An interim decision: the species patent was held vulnerable to revocation, not revoked.

slides.part: Chapter 10: Case Briefs
slides.title: Risdiplam: the facts and the central question
slides.html:
In the risdiplam case (2025) Roche sued on its species patent while relying on genus coverage, which raised the defining question of Part C: disclosure, or mere coverage?

F. Hoffmann La Roche v. Natco Pharma (risdiplam), Delhi High Court, 2025

Citation
Single Judge: CS(COMM) 567/2024, Delhi High Court, 24 March 2025. Division Bench: FAO(OS)(COMM) 43/2025, C. Hari Shankar and Ajay Digpaul JJ., 9 October 2025; 2025:DHC:8943 DB.
Facts
  1. Risdiplam is an oral small molecule treatment for spinal muscular atrophy (SMA), a leading genetic cause of infant mortality.
  2. Roche held Indian patent IN 334397 claiming risdiplam, and earlier genus documents (WO ’916 and US ’955) whose Markush formula covered it.
  3. Roche sued Natco, which was preparing to launch a generic, relying on genus level coverage.
  4. Natco challenged validity under Section 107 read with Section 64(1)(e) (novelty) and 64(1)(f) (obviousness).
  5. In the United States, Roche had sued Natco on the genus patent US ’955 and had treated risdiplam as covered by it in a patent term extension application.
Central question
Did the earlier genus patent disclose risdiplam as a specific compound, or merely cover it within a vast chemical space?
Issues
(1) Anticipation: disclosure or mere coverage? (2) Obviousness over the genus documents. (3) Credible challenge sufficient to refuse an injunction. (4) Scope of appellate interference.

Table 11: Case brief: F. Hoffmann La Roche v. Natco Pharma (risdiplam)

Compare Boehringer: there too the patentee’s own assertion of genus coverage was turned against it. Roche’s United States conduct plays that role here.

slides.part: Chapter 10: Case Briefs
slides.title: Risdiplam: not anticipated, but obvious
slides.html:
The single judge found credible anticipation and obviousness; the Division Bench held that coverage is not disclosure but found risdiplam prima facie obvious. Either way, no injunction.

F. Hoffmann La Roche v. Natco Pharma (2025): reasoning and result

Reasoning: Single Judge
Natco had raised a credible challenge. A “person in the know” could arrive at risdiplam from the genus patent, so there was a credible case of anticipation; Roche’s own conduct in the United States supported the view that risdiplam was disclosed. A credible obviousness challenge was also made out. Public interest favoured Natco, which would manufacture in India at a fraction of Roche’s price.
Reasoning: Division Bench
Coverage and disclosure are not synonymous. A genus patent covering millions of compounds within a Markush claim does not thereby disclose each species; for anticipation the species must be specifically disclosed, not merely mathematically encompassed. Infringement turns on coverage, anticipation on disclosure, and the Bench doubted the broad proposition in AstraZeneca v. Intas. It was not prima facie inclined to find anticipation under Section 64(1)(e). But on obviousness, the only structural difference between risdiplam and Compound 809 (disclosed in WO ’916 and US ’955) is the replacement of a CH group by a nitrogen atom at one position; with common inventors and similar chemical teaching, risdiplam was prima facie obvious under Section 64(1)(f). The single judge had applied the correct tests, and the finding of a credible challenge was not open to interference.
Judgment
Appeal dismissed; interim injunction refused. Natco’s product was priced at about ₹15,900 a bottle against roughly ₹6 lakh for Roche’s.

Exam tip. Write that risdiplam was held prima facie obvious, not anticipated, at the appellate stage. The “inherent disclosure” view (anticipation by inherent derivation from the genus) belongs to the single judge.

Law update. The Supreme Court declined interim relief to Roche in October 2025, and the suit continues to trial.

slides.part: Chapter 10: Case Briefs
slides.title: Semaglutide: double patenting exposed
slides.html:
Novo Nordisk (2025 to 2026) pitted a semaglutide species patent against an expired genus patent, and Novo’s own foreign filings and Indian statements became evidence against it.

Novo Nordisk A/S v. Dr. Reddy’s Laboratories Ltd. (semaglutide), Delhi High Court

Citation
Novo Nordisk A/S v. Dr. Reddy’s Laboratories Ltd. and Anr., CS(COMM) 565/2025, Delhi High Court. Single Judge order: 2 December 2025. The Division Bench refused to stay it in December 2025 and dismissed the appeal on 9 March 2026.
Facts
  1. Semaglutide is the blockbuster GLP 1 receptor agonist for type 2 diabetes and obesity.
  2. Novo held species patent IN 262697 claiming semaglutide (priority date 18 March 2005) and an earlier genus patent, IN 275964, filed in 2003 and since expired.
  3. Dr. Reddy’s imported and exported semaglutide and wished to make it in India for export to countries where Novo held no patent. Novo sued.
  4. Dr. Reddy’s challenged validity under Section 64(1)(a), (e), (f) and (k) and raised the Gillette defence (its activity fell within an expired patent).
  5. Novo had obtained term extensions abroad for both the genus and species patents, and its Form 27 statements in India declared semaglutide as worked under both.
  6. Novo argued that the genus patent, published on 31 March 2005, could not be prior art for a species patent with an 18 March 2005 priority date.
Issues
(1) Did the genus patent claim or disclose semaglutide, supporting revocation for prior claiming (Section 64(1)(a)) or lack of novelty (Section 64(1)(e))? (2) Was semaglutide obvious (Section 64(1)(f))? (3) Should an interim injunction issue?

Table 12: Case brief: Novo Nordisk v. Dr. Reddy’s Laboratories (semaglutide)

Hold three pieces of evidence in mind for the reasoning: Novo’s internal records from 2004, its term extensions abroad and its Form 27 statements.

slides.part: Chapter 10: Case Briefs
slides.title: Semaglutide: withholding, identity of claims and obviousness
slides.html:
The single judge inferred intentional withholding and found credible challenges on three grounds; the Division Bench rejected prior claiming for want of identical claims but upheld refusal on obviousness.

Novo Nordisk v. Dr. Reddy’s Laboratories (2025 to 2026): reasoning and result

Reasoning: Single Judge
The “invented in 2004” revelation: internal project timelines and prosecution histories showed that Novo had identified semaglutide as the lead compound by 2004, while the genus patent was being prosecuted, yet withheld it for a separate, later species application. The Court drew an inference of intentional withholding: the species data existed and was known when the genus was filed, and its omission was a strategic choice, not an oversight (evergreening). Credible challenges were found under Section 64(1)(a), (e) and (f); the genus disclosures enabled a skilled person to reach semaglutide; the term extension filings and Form 27 statements were treated as admissions; non disclosure of material facts was noted.
Reasoning: Division Bench
A credible challenge was made out, but not under Section 64(1)(a). Prior claiming requires identity of claims, and the genus patent did not claim semaglutide as such; the skilled person has no role under Section 64(1)(a). The challenge relates to Section 64(1)(e) and especially 64(1)(f): from the perspective of a “person in the know”, semaglutide was prima facie obvious from the genus patent. Dr. Reddy’s undertook not to sell in India during the appeal.
Judgment
Interim injunction refused; appeal dismissed. A landmark blow to the global evergreening strategy.

Exam tip. Three points.

  1. At the interim stage the courts found a credible challenge, not invalidity.
  2. Section 64(1)(a) is prior claiming, not anticipation by disclosure (that is Section 64(1)(e)).
  3. The Division Bench rejected the Section 64(1)(a) ground and rested on Sections 64(1)(e) and (f).

slides.part: Chapter 10: Case Briefs
slides.title: United States standards: Graham and Amgen
slides.html:
Two US Supreme Court cases set the American benchmarks: Graham (1966) frames obviousness under § 103, and Amgen (2023) demands that a genus claim enable its full scope.

ElementGraham v. John Deere Co. (1966)Amgen Inc. v. Sanofi (2023)
Citation383 U.S. 1 (1966).598 U.S. 594 (2023), decided 18 May 2023; unanimous; Gorsuch J.
FactsPatents on agricultural plough equipment and other devices were challenged as obvious.Amgen claimed, by function, every antibody that binds particular residues on the PCSK9 protein and blocks it from binding LDL receptors, potentially millions of antibodies. The specification gave the sequences of 26 antibodies and methods for finding more.
IssueHow is obviousness under § 103 to be decided?Did the specification enable the full scope of the functional genus claims under § 112(a)?
ReasoningObviousness is a legal question resting on four factual inquiries: (1) the scope and content of the prior art; (2) the differences between the prior art and the claims; (3) the level of ordinary skill in the art; (4) secondary considerations such as commercial success and long felt need.A genus patent must enable the full scope of its claims: the more a patentee claims, the more it must enable. Amgen’s methods amounted to trial and error research assignments.
JudgmentEstablished the framework still used for obviousness.Claims invalid for lack of enablement. Broad claims require broad enablement.

Table 13: Graham v. John Deere and Amgen v. Sanofi

Remember: Graham’s four inquiries run S, D, L, S: Scope and content of the prior art, Differences from the claims, Level of ordinary skill, Secondary considerations.

slides.part: Chapter 10: Case Briefs
slides.title: US limits on broad and serial claims
slides.html:
Beyond Graham and Amgen, US law polices genus claims and serial filings through a high enablement burden, obviousness type double patenting and terminal disclaimers.

  1. High enablement burden: undue experimentation is prohibited, and genus claims in biotechnology face heightened scrutiny.
  2. Obviousness type double patenting (ODP): the United States doctrine that stops a patentee extending its term through a second patent on an obvious variant; a functional parallel to India’s approach.
  3. Terminal disclaimers: a procedural tool to overcome ODP rejections by tying the later patent’s expiry to the earlier one.

Read ODP alongside Boehringer: both stop a patentee stretching one invention into a longer monopoly by filing again, whether on an obvious variant (ODP) or on the same inventive concept (one patent for one inventive concept).

Law update. The USPTO proposed stricter rules on terminal disclaimers in 2024, but the proposal was withdrawn in December 2024.

slides.part: Chapter 10: Case Briefs
slides.title: AstraZeneca v. Intas: asserting the genus
slides.html:
AstraZeneca v. Intas (2021) stops a patentee having it both ways: a product it says infringes its genus patent must be treated as disclosed in that genus.

AstraZeneca AB v. Intas Pharmaceuticals (dapagliflozin), Delhi High Court (Division Bench), 2021

A Delhi High Court Division Bench decision of 2021 on AstraZeneca’s dapagliflozin patents. It is cited for the proposition that once a patentee claims that a product infringes its earlier genus patent, that product must be treated as disclosed in the genus patent.

  1. Followed: Boehringer (2023).
  2. Doubted: the Roche v. Natco Division Bench (2025).

It is also associated with the inventor’s knowledge standard: when assessing whether a species was obvious at the time of the genus filing, the relevant knowledge is not that of an average skilled person but of the inventors themselves. Scientists who designed a genus know its chemical space intimately and cannot claim ignorance of compounds they probably synthesised and tested during lead optimisation.

The phrase “person in the know” itself appears in the risdiplam single judge decision and in the semaglutide Division Bench decision.

Exam focus. Cite AstraZeneca with its later history, and keep the notes’ caution: the inventor’s knowledge standard is only “associated with” this case, while the phrase “person in the know” comes from the 2025 decisions.

slides.part: Chapter 10: Case Briefs
slides.title: Public access: Natco v. Bayer and Roche v. Cipla
slides.html:
Two earlier cases put public access at the centre: India’s first compulsory licence (2012) and a refused interim injunction against generic erlotinib (2008).

Natco Pharma v. Bayer: the first Indian compulsory licence (Controller of Patents, 2012)

The Controller of Patents granted India’s first compulsory licence on 9 March 2012, on Natco’s application under Section 84, for Bayer’s Nexavar (sorafenib), a kidney and liver cancer drug.

Natco was to sell at a price of about 3% of Bayer’s price (roughly ₹8,880 a month against ₹2,80,428) and pay a royalty, initially 6% of net sales.

Bayer’s challenges failed before the Intellectual Property Appellate Board and the Bombay High Court (Bayer Corporation v. Union of India, 2014), and the Supreme Court declined to interfere. The licence established that public access is a legally enforceable right, not merely an aspiration.

Exam tip. Cite it as Natco v. Bayer (Controller, 2012) and Bayer Corporation v. Union of India (Bombay High Court). The “3%” refers to Natco’s price compared with Bayer’s, not to the royalty.

F. Hoffmann La Roche v. Cipla: erlotinib (2008 to 2012)

The Delhi High Court refused an interim injunction against Cipla’s generic erlotinib (Roche’s Tarceva) in March 2008, and a Division Bench upheld the refusal in April 2009, expressly weighing the public interest in affordable, life saving cancer treatment against Roche’s commercial interests.

The suit was decided in 2012, with a further appeal decided in 2015. The case is cited for the weight given to public interest at the interim stage.

slides.part: Chapter 11: Doctrinal Developments and Comparative Perspectives
slides.title: The person in the know
slides.html:
The 2025 Indian decisions reframed the skilled person: the question is no longer what an average chemist would discover, but what the genus inventors themselves already knew.

One of the most significant doctrinal contributions of the 2025 Indian decisions is the reframing of the PHOSITA (person having ordinary skill in the art) standard in genus and species disputes.

Traditional PHOSITAPerson in the know
WhoA skilled but unimaginative technician with general knowledge of the fieldThe inventors of the genus patent, presumed to have known about the species
The questionWhat would an average chemist discover?What did the actual inventors already know?
Where usedThe standard test in most obviousness determinations worldwideThe risdiplam single judge decision and the semaglutide Division Bench decision

Practical consequence: bioisosteric substitutions, such as swapping a carbon hydrogen (CH) group for a nitrogen (N) atom, are treated as obvious to medicinal chemists, which forecloses species claims built on such changes.

Why the shift makes sense: the scientists who designed a genus know its chemical space intimately (the inventor’s knowledge standard in Chapter 10), so the law asks what they knew instead of imagining an outsider.

slides.part: Chapter 11: Doctrinal Developments and Comparative Perspectives
slides.title: Bioisosteres and the narrowing species patent
slides.html:
Medicinal chemists routinely swap bioisosteres, so courts now treat such swaps as prima facie obvious, which sharply narrows the room for legitimate small molecule species patents.

The person in the know standard is a seismic shift beyond the conventional PHOSITA framework. The reason lies in how drugs are actually optimised.

Bioisosteres
Atoms or groups of similar size, shape and electronic properties. Medicinal chemistry textbooks teach that they are routinely interchanged during drug optimisation.

Substituting nitrogen for a CH group, as in risdiplam, is a standard technique, and courts now treat such substitutions as prima facie obvious. This sharply narrows the space for legitimate species patents in small molecule drug development.

Scientific note. A bioisostere can replace another atom or group while keeping broadly similar biological activity; a CH to N swap in an aromatic ring is a classic example. Such a change can still alter solubility, metabolism, binding or toxicity, so patentees argue that its effect is not always predictable. Obviousness therefore remains a question of evidence in each case: in risdiplam the court relied on the single CH to N difference from a disclosed compound, common inventors and similar teaching.

slides.part: Chapter 11: Doctrinal Developments and Comparative Perspectives
slides.title: The inherent disclosure trap
slides.html:
A genus patent can trap its owner: if the species is a predictable evolution of the genus, the genus may be treated as disclosing it and defeat the species patent.

  1. The Markush problem: a Markush group can cover billions of compounds through combinatorial chemistry. Courts ask whether the species is a predictable evolution of the genus that a medicinal chemist would reach through routine optimisation; if so, the genus may be treated as implicitly disclosing it.
  2. The risdiplam lesson: the single judge treated the N for CH swap within a disclosed scaffold as anticipation by inherent derivation from the genus. On appeal the Division Bench accepted that coverage is not disclosure and decided the case on obviousness instead.
  3. The strategic warning: counsel must advise that a genus patent, once filed, may defeat later species applications. The safer course is to file species protection alongside the genus, or risk losing it where the compound is a predictable derivative, whether through an anticipation or an obviousness attack.

Exam focus. “Inherent derivation” is the single judge’s view in risdiplam. The Division Bench decided on obviousness, so never write that the appellate court held risdiplam anticipated.

slides.part: Chapter 11: Doctrinal Developments and Comparative Perspectives
slides.title: Coverage versus disclosure
slides.html:
Coverage governs infringement; disclosure governs anticipation. A patentee cannot read its genus widely to catch a generic and narrowly to save its own species patent.

Arguably the most consequential doctrinal distinction in contemporary pharmaceutical patent law, applied in the risdiplam case.

COVERAGEDISCLOSURE
PictureA vast lattice: every compound within the Markush groupA room with a few specific objects: the specific embodiments
MeaningCompounds falling within the words of the Markush claimSpecific compounds described sufficiently for a skilled person to reproduce
GovernsInfringement analysisValidity (anticipation) analysis
Why it mattersA generic manufacturer whose compound falls within the structural scope of a Markush genus claim infringes, even if that molecule was never individually made or described in the genus patent.A species patent is invalid for anticipation only if the species was specifically disclosed, not merely encompassed, in the prior genus patent. This has protected some species patents from early invalidation.

Table 14: Coverage and disclosure

The tension: a patentee wants a wide reading of coverage when suing (so the generic falls within the genus) and a narrow reading of disclosure when defending the species patent (so the genus does not anticipate it). Boehringer and AstraZeneca stopped patentees from having it both ways; the Roche Division Bench restated the distinction but decided against Roche on obviousness.

Remember: coverage is the lattice and decides infringement; disclosure is the room and decides anticipation.

slides.part: Chapter 11: Doctrinal Developments and Comparative Perspectives
slides.title: Europe: sufficiency and inventive step
slides.html:
The European Patent Office tackles the problem through sufficiency of disclosure and inventive step, with case law that increasingly mirrors Indian disclosure expectations.

The European Patent Office approaches the problem through Article 83 EPC (sufficiency of disclosure) and Article 56 EPC (inventive step).

Article 83 EPC. The disclosure must be clear and complete enough for a skilled person to carry out the invention across the full claimed scope. For a broad genus, the specification must enable the entire claimed class, not just preferred examples, and this is increasingly used against overbroad genus claims.

Technical contribution versus legal drafting: Europe treats the technical contribution to the art as the measure of patentability. A species that is merely a predictable variant of the genus, even if it performs better, is not inventive unless the improvement was unexpected and surprising.

Two tools apply this on inventive step:

  1. The problem and solution approach to inventive step.
  2. In selection inventions, asking whether the selected compound was individually disclosed and whether the selection shows a technical effect.

Caveat. The EPC is a separate treaty administered by the EPO, not European Union law. Write “EPC” or “EPO”, never “EU law”.

slides.part: Chapter 11: Doctrinal Developments and Comparative Perspectives
slides.title: The judicial role: guardians of public access
slides.html:
Indian courts treat access to medicines as a constitutional value: Article 21 shapes the public interest test, and for life saving drugs it weighs heavily against the patentee.

The constitutional dimension

Indian courts anchor public interest analysis in patent cases in Article 21 of the Constitution, the right to life, read to include the right to health and access to affordable medicines. Patent exclusivity that obstructs this right faces judicial scepticism at every stage of litigation.

“Superadded” public interest

In cases on life saving drugs, the harm from denying generic access to critical medicines is treated as outweighing the harm to a patentee from delayed enforcement of a commercially motivated species claim (see Natco v. Bayer, Roche v. Cipla and the risdiplam case).

slides.part: Chapter 11: Doctrinal Developments and Comparative Perspectives
slides.title: Synthesis: the new paradigm
slides.html:
Indian, US and European case law from 2013 to 2025 closes the era of unchallenged evergreening: the inventive concept and the evidence, not claim drafting, now decide species patents.

The combined effect of Indian, United States and European case law from 2013 to 2025 is a fundamental recalibration of pharmaceutical patent law: the era of unchallenged evergreening through strategic species filings is closing.

  1. Old paradigm: formal claims set patentability; a broad genus protects the species.
  2. Transitional phase: courts demand disclosure; Section 3(d) and scrutiny rise.
  3. New paradigm: inventive concept and evidence steer prosecution; no double patenting.

Figure 2: From the old to the new paradigm

  1. Obviousness as the primary tool: evergreening is blocked through heightened obviousness analysis, not only Section 3(d).
  2. Inventive concept focus: courts look past legal drafting to the underlying scientific idea and ask whether it was truly new.
  3. Evidence based prosecution: internal timelines, project records and foreign prosecution histories are now fair game in Indian proceedings (semaglutide: internal timelines, Form 27 and foreign term extensions; risdiplam: United States filings).

slides.part: Quick revision
slides.title: Part C in one page
slides.html:
A genus covers a class and a species claims one member; India meets evergreening with Section 3(d) and with revocation grounds raised at the interim stage.

  1. A genus patent covers a class of compounds, often through a Markush formula; a species patent claims one member.
  2. Evergreening uses later species or derivative patents to extend exclusivity.
  3. India meets it with Section 3(d) (Novartis, 2013) and, increasingly, with revocation grounds raised as defences at the interim stage.
  4. Boehringer (2023) refused an injunction on linagliptin: one patent for one inventive concept.
  5. In Roche v. Natco (2025) the Division Bench accepted that coverage is not disclosure but found risdiplam prima facie obvious over Compound 809.
  6. In Novo Nordisk (2025 and 2026) the Division Bench held that prior claiming needs identity of claims, but upheld refusal of an injunction on semaglutide for obviousness from the standpoint of a person in the know.
  7. In the United States, Graham sets the obviousness framework and Amgen requires enablement of the full genus; in Europe, Articles 83 and 56 EPC play the equivalent roles.

Common mistakes. Avoid these four:

  1. Saying a species patent was “held invalid” in an interim decision: the courts found only a credible challenge.
  2. Treating Section 64(1)(a) (prior claiming) as anticipation by disclosure, which is Section 64(1)(e).
  3. Describing the EPC as European Union law.
  4. Stating that the Roche Division Bench held risdiplam anticipated: it held it prima facie obvious.
