slides.title: Practice questions
slides.html:
1. Short answer: Distinguish a genus patent from a species patent. What is a Markush claim?
  2. Short answer: State the four Graham factors.
  3. Short answer: What did the Division Bench hold in Roche v. Natco on novelty and on obviousness?
  4. Short answer: Why did the Division Bench in Novo Nordisk reject the Section 64(1)(a) ground?
  5. Short answer: Distinguish coverage from disclosure.
  6. Analytical: “Infringement is predicated on coverage; anticipation is predicated on disclosure.” Discuss with reference to Boehringer, Roche v. Natco and Novo Nordisk.
  7. Analytical: Is the “person in the know” a legitimate refinement of the PHOSITA or a departure from the statute? Discuss.
  8. Analytical: Compare enablement under § 112 after Amgen, sufficiency under Article 83 EPC and Section 3(d) of the Patents Act.
  9. Problem question: X Pharma obtained a genus patent in 2006 covering 50 million compounds. In 2008 it filed a species patent on compound Z, which differs from Example 12 of the genus patent only by a CH to N replacement. The genus patent has now expired. X Pharma sues Y, an Indian generic company, for infringing the species patent and seeks an interim injunction. In earlier litigation abroad, X Pharma asserted that Z fell within its genus patent. Advise Y.

slides.part: Answer plans
slides.title: Answer plans: Q1 and Q2
slides.html:
Short answers score when they define first, state the rule exactly, and name the case with its citation; these two plans show the order.

Q1. Distinguish a genus patent from a species patent. What is a Markush claim?

  1. Define a genus patent: a broad structural claim, often a Markush group, covering a large class of compounds sharing a common scaffold; it can capture thousands of molecules in one filing.
  2. Define a species patent: a later, specific claim to one compound in the genus, often the most pharmacologically active, filed after clinical data confirms superior efficacy.
  3. Explain the Markush claim: a scaffold with variable positions (R1, R2), each with listed substituents; every combination is claimed, so one formula covers millions though only a few are described and tested. Named after Eugene Markush (1920s).
  4. Use the illustration: three positions with 100 groups each cover one million compounds.
  5. Close with the central legal question, genuine invention or obvious extension, and one real pair (risdiplam: WO ’916 and US ’955, then IN 334397).

Q2. State the four Graham factors.

  1. Cite Graham v. John Deere Co., 383 U.S. 1 (1966): obviousness under § 103 is a legal question resting on four factual inquiries.
  2. List them in order: (1) scope and content of the prior art; (2) differences between the prior art and the claims; (3) level of ordinary skill in the art; (4) secondary considerations such as commercial success and long felt need.
  3. Add one line of context: the framework is still used for obviousness, which is separate from enablement under § 112 (Amgen).

slides.part: Answer plans
slides.title: Answer plans: Q3 and Q4
slides.html:
Both questions ask what a Division Bench held, so state the ground of decision precisely and name the ground the Bench rejected.

Q3. What did the Division Bench hold in Roche v. Natco on novelty and on obviousness?

  1. Set the facts in two lines: risdiplam for SMA; Roche’s IN 334397; genus WO ’916 and US ’955; Natco’s challenge under Section 107 read with Section 64(1)(e) and (f).
  2. Novelty: coverage and disclosure are not synonymous; anticipation needs specific disclosure, not mathematical encompassing. The Bench doubted AstraZeneca v. Intas and was not prima facie inclined to find anticipation under Section 64(1)(e).
  3. Obviousness: the only difference from Compound 809 is a CH to N replacement at one position; with common inventors and similar teaching, risdiplam was prima facie obvious under Section 64(1)(f).
  4. Conclude: the single judge’s credible challenge finding was not open to interference; appeal dismissed, injunction refused. Never write “held anticipated”.

Q4. Why did the Division Bench in Novo Nordisk reject the Section 64(1)(a) ground?

  1. Define Section 64(1)(a): revocation where the invention was claimed in a valid claim of earlier priority date in another Indian patent (prior claiming).
  2. Give the facts briefly: genus IN 275964 (filed 2003, expired); species IN 262697 on semaglutide (priority 18 March 2005); the single judge had found credible challenges under Section 64(1)(a), (e) and (f).
  3. State the reason: prior claiming requires identity of claims; the genus patent did not claim semaglutide as such; the skilled person has no role under Section 64(1)(a).
  4. Show where the challenge succeeded instead: Section 64(1)(e) and especially (f), semaglutide being prima facie obvious to a “person in the know”.
  5. Conclude with the common mistake: Section 64(1)(a) is prior claiming, not anticipation by disclosure, which is Section 64(1)(e).

slides.part: Answer plans
slides.title: Answer plans: Q5 and Q6
slides.html:
Coverage and disclosure appear twice: once as a short distinction, once as an essay. Use the same definitions, then add the cases in order for the essay.

Q5. Distinguish coverage from disclosure.

  1. Define coverage: compounds falling within the words of the Markush claim (the vast lattice); it governs infringement.
  2. Define disclosure: specific compounds described sufficiently for a skilled person to reproduce (the room with a few objects); it governs anticipation.
  3. Explain why it matters: a generic within the genus scope infringes even if its molecule was never made or described; a species is anticipated only if specifically disclosed, which has protected some species patents.
  4. State the tension: wide coverage when suing, narrow disclosure when defending; Boehringer and AstraZeneca stopped patentees having it both ways.
  5. Conclude with Roche v. Natco (Division Bench): the distinction was restated, but Roche still lost on obviousness.

Q6. “Infringement is predicated on coverage; anticipation is predicated on disclosure.” Discuss with reference to Boehringer, Roche v. Natco and Novo Nordisk.

  1. Introduce the distinction (Table 14) and the patentee’s temptation to read the genus widely to sue and narrowly to defend.
  2. Boehringer (2023): following AstraZeneca, a patentee that sued on the genus could not deny that linagliptin was disclosed; species patent prima facie vulnerable; one patent for one inventive concept.
  3. Roche v. Natco (2025): the single judge found credible anticipation, relying on Roche’s United States conduct; the Division Bench adopted the statement in the question, doubted AstraZeneca, and decided on obviousness (CH to N over Compound 809).
  4. Novo Nordisk (2025 to 2026): the single judge treated term extension filings and Form 27 statements as admissions; the Division Bench required identity of claims for Section 64(1)(a) and rested on Section 64(1)(e) and (f).
  5. Evaluate: the distinction shields species patents from anticipation, but obviousness, the person in the know and the patentee’s own admissions now do the work; recall Novartis on the gap between what a patent covers and what it discloses.
  6. Conclude: the statement is sound doctrine, but it no longer saves strategic species filings.

slides.part: Answer plans
slides.title: Answer plans: Q7 and Q8
slides.html:
Weigh both sides before concluding on Q7; for Q8, apply one frame to all three regimes.

Q7. Is the “person in the know” a legitimate refinement of the PHOSITA or a departure from the statute?

  1. Define the traditional PHOSITA (a skilled but unimaginative technician) and the person in the know (what the genus inventors already knew).
  2. Trace its source: the inventor’s knowledge standard associated with AstraZeneca v. Intas; the phrase appears in the risdiplam single judge decision and the semaglutide Division Bench decision.
  3. For refinement: genus inventors know its chemical space and cannot claim ignorance of compounds they probably synthesised; CH to N swaps are routine; internal timelines and foreign filings prove what they knew.
  4. For departure: the notes call it a seismic shift beyond the PHOSITA framework, and a CH to N swap can alter solubility, metabolism, binding or toxicity. Test it against Section 2(1)(ja) and Section 64(1)(f).
  5. Note the limit in Novo Nordisk: under Section 64(1)(a) the skilled person has no role.
  6. Conclude: defensible as a refinement where evidence shows common inventors and similar teaching, because obviousness remains a question of evidence.

Q8. Compare enablement under § 112 after Amgen, sufficiency under Article 83 EPC and Section 3(d) of the Patents Act.

  1. Frame the answer: three regimes respond to one problem, a genus that claims more than it discloses (Table 7).
  2. United States: § 112 enablement; Amgen (2023) struck down functional claims to every PCSK9 blocking antibody, backed by 26 sequences and trial and error methods. The more one claims, the more one must enable; obviousness stays under § 103.
  3. Europe: Article 83 EPC requires disclosure across the full claimed scope, not just preferred examples; Article 56 EPC asks for an unexpected and surprising improvement. The EPC is not EU law.
  4. India: Section 3(d) filters the later patent, refusing new forms of known substances without significantly enhanced therapeutic efficacy (Novartis), backed by Section 64(1) grounds through Section 107.
  5. Conclude: § 112 and Article 83 attack the breadth of the genus, Section 3(d) the later derivative; all three look to the inventive concept, not drafting.

slides.part: Answer plans
slides.title: Answer plan: the X Pharma problem
slides.html:
Answer the problem in the notes’ own Issues, Rules, Application and Conclusion order, and rank the grounds: obviousness first, then evidence of disclosure, then Section 3(d).

Q9. Problem: X Pharma’s expired genus patent (2006, 50 million compounds) and species patent on Z (2008, one CH to N change from Example 12). Advise Y.

  1. Issues: a credible challenge under Section 107 read with Section 64(1)(a), (e) and (f); Section 3(d); whether an interim injunction should be refused.
  2. Rules: Sections 3(d), 64(1)(a), (e), (f) and 107; Novartis; Boehringer (one inventive concept; consequence of asserting the genus); Roche v. Natco (coverage is not disclosure; CH to N obviousness; person in the know); Novo Nordisk (identity of claims for Section 64(1)(a); use of foreign filings and internal records).
  3. Application: prior claiming is unlikely unless the genus claims Z as such. Anticipation needs specific disclosure, though X Pharma’s foreign assertion is evidence of disclosure (Boehringer).
  4. The strongest ground is obviousness over Example 12, given a single bioisosteric change, especially if the inventors overlap. Section 3(d) applies if Z is a derivative of a known substance and no enhanced therapeutic efficacy is shown. Public interest and price weigh against an injunction.
  5. Conclusion: Y has a strong credible challenge, chiefly on obviousness; an interim injunction is likely to be refused, subject to the evidence at trial.

Exam focus. Say “credible challenge”, never “invalid”: this is an interim injunction application, and the answer is subject to the evidence at trial.

slides.part: Chapter 13: The Concept of a Geographical Indication
slides.title: Indication of source, GI and appellation of origin
slides.html:
A GI expresses a product and place linkage; indication of source, GI and appellation of origin are three nested circles, differing in how strongly the place shapes the product.

TRIPS recognised GIs. A GI expresses a product and place linkage: it is a means to protect the origin of the product.

Before GIs, the relevant ideas were the indication of origin, the indication of source (IoS) and the appellation of origin (AO). Such products were protected by individual trade marks and by laws against unfair trade practices.

The three concepts differ in one thing: what ties the product to the place. Read the table from the weakest tie to the strongest.

ConceptWhat links the product to the placeExample
Indication of source (outer circle)Only the fact that the product is made there; no quality or reputation link."Made in India", "Made in China"
Geographical indication (middle circle)The reputation, characteristics or quality of the product stem from the very fact that it is produced in that place.Darjeeling tea
Appellation of origin (inner circle)All raw materials, the manufacturing process, labour and skill originate from the place; quality and characteristics are due exclusively or essentially to the geographical environment, including natural and human factors.Lisbon Agreement appellations

Notes reference: Table 15: IoS, GI and AO as concentric circles.

Because the circles are nested, every appellation of origin is a GI, and every GI is an indication of source, but not the other way round. "Made in India" tells you only where a thing was made; "Darjeeling" on tea tells you that the tea's qualities come from where it was produced.

Remember: three circles, from the outside in: Source, then GI, then Appellation. Each inner circle needs a stronger tie to the place.

slides.part: Chapter 13: The Concept of a Geographical Indication
slides.title: GI versus trade mark, and the US trade mark route
slides.html:
A trade mark points to an enterprise, a GI points to a place and the qualities it gives, which is why a GI is a community right over goods.

The United States approach: the USA had no separate GI system. To meet its international obligations it protects GIs through trade mark law (certification and collective marks), taking the view that another statute would be a burden and that the existing system is capable of protecting GIs. Darjeeling tea, for example, is protected in the USA as a certification mark.

So the two rights can overlap. In India, though, they are separate systems, and the differences below decide cases.

Geographical indicationTrade markExplanation
Origin and source identificationSource identificationA trade mark identifies the trade source (an enterprise); a GI identifies geographical origin and the qualities linked to it.
Geographical originProprietor basedEvery producer in the area meeting the standard may use a GI; a trade mark is owned by a proprietor.
GoodsGoods and servicesUnder the Indian GI Act only goods can carry a GI (relevant in Tea Board v. ITC, a lounge).
Community rightIndividual or community rightCollective and certification marks let trade mark law serve groups too.
Mostly generic names with a location name are protectedGeneric names cannot be registeredA GI often joins a place name to the common name of the product ("Darjeeling" plus tea), which trade mark law would treat as descriptive.

Notes reference: Table 16: GI and trade mark compared.

GI tag: an assurance of origin to avoid deception.

Exam focus. The goods-only row matters in practice. A hotel lounge is a service, which is why naming one "Darjeeling" fell outside GI protection in Tea Board v. ITC (chapter 15).

slides.part: Chapter 13: The Concept of a Geographical Indication
slides.title: The Parmesan case (Commission v. Germany)
slides.html:
Selling non-conforming cheese as "Parmesan" evokes the PDO "Parmigiano Reggiano", which EU law prohibits, yet the Commission's case against Germany still failed for want of proof.

The Parmesan case is also called the "Italy and Denmark case"; Italy and Denmark intervened on opposite sides.

Commission of the European Communities v. Federal Republic of Germany, Case C 132/05

Citation
Commission of the European Communities v. Federal Republic of Germany, Case C 132/05, Court of Justice (Grand Chamber), 26 February 2008. Italy (with the Czech Republic) supported the Commission; Denmark (with Austria) supported Germany.
Facts
Cheese not made to the specification of the protected designation of origin (PDO) "Parmigiano Reggiano" was sold in Germany as "Parmesan". The Commission argued that "Parmesan" is a translation of the PDO and that Germany failed to stop the misuse.
Issue
Does use of "Parmesan" for such cheese infringe the PDO, and was Germany obliged to act against it of its own motion?
Holding
Use of "Parmesan" for cheese not meeting the PDO specification is an evocation of the PDO, which EU law prohibits, so whether it is a translation is irrelevant. Germany failed to show that "Parmesan" had become generic. But the Commission did not prove that German law failed to protect the PDO, so the infringement action against Germany was dismissed.
Exam tip
The question is whether the name "Parmesan" infringes the PDO "Parmigiano Reggiano" (it does, by evocation), not whether "parma cheese" violates "parmesan cheese".

Notes reference: Table 17: Case brief: Commission v. Germany (Parmesan).

Read the holding in two steps. On the law, the name loses: evocation, using a term that calls the protected name to mind, is enough, without translation or confusion. On the procedure, the Commission loses: it had to prove that German law failed to protect the PDO, and it did not.

slides.part: Chapter 14: The International Framework
slides.title: Paris Convention, 1883
slides.html:
The Paris Convention first named indications of source and appellations of origin as industrial property, but reached only false indications, leaving sanctions to national law where seizure is not allowed.

The Paris Convention for the Protection of Industrial Property, 1883 is the starting point. Its provisions on indications:

ProvisionContent
Article 1(2) and (3)Indications of source and appellations of origin are listed among the objects of industrial property, the first time these terms were used. Industrial property is understood in the broadest sense, covering industrial and agricultural goods.
Articles 9 and 10Seizure on importation of goods bearing a false indication of source (or a false identity of the producer); where national law does not allow seizure, any other action or remedy the affected country's law provides.
Article 10bisEffective protection against unfair competition, meaning acts contrary to honest practices, including acts creating confusion, false allegations discrediting a competitor, and indications liable to mislead the public as to the nature, manufacturing process, characteristics, suitability or quantity of goods.
Protection against false or misleading indications as unfair competitionAchieved through Articles 10 and 10bis, with remedies under Article 10ter.
Article 19Members may make special agreements among themselves for the protection of industrial property (the Madrid and Lisbon Agreements are examples).

Notes reference: Table 18: Paris Convention provisions on indications.

Correction. The Convention has no Article 11bis; Article 11 concerns temporary protection at international exhibitions.

Limitations of the Paris Convention:

  1. appellation of origin and indication of source are not defined;
  2. it deals only with false indications, not misleading ones;
  3. it does not deal with genericide of an indication outside the home country;
  4. where a country's laws do not permit seizure on importation, sanctions are left to national law.

Each gap explains the next instrument: Madrid adds deceptive indications, Lisbon defines appellations and stops them becoming generic abroad, and TRIPS defines GIs and sets minimum standards.

slides.part: Chapter 14: The International Framework
slides.title: Madrid (1891) and Lisbon (1958) Agreements
slides.html:
Two special agreements under Paris Article 19 went further: Madrid reached deceptive indications, and Lisbon gave appellations of origin a definition and an international register.

Madrid Agreement (Madrid Agreement for the Repression of False or Deceptive Indications of Source on Goods, 1891). It was created in response to proposals of Paris signatories for more comprehensive regulation.

  1. Article 1 provides for seizure on importation of goods bearing a false or deceptive indication naming a member country or a place in it, going beyond Article 10 of Paris.
  2. Article 3bis extends the prohibition to deceptive publicity.
  3. Article 4 leaves it to national courts to decide which names are generic, except regional appellations for products of the vine. So a national court cannot treat a wine region's name as generic.

Lisbon Agreement (Lisbon Agreement for the Protection of Appellations of Origin and their International Registration, 1958):

  1. It adopts the French definition: an appellation whose quality and characteristics are due exclusively or essentially to the geographical environment, including natural and human factors.
  2. Registration is at the International Bureau of WIPO, provided the appellation is recognised and protected in its home country.
  3. No protected appellation can be deemed generic in another member country so long as it is protected in its country of origin.
  4. Limitation: it is confined to nations that protect appellations of origin as such.

Law update. The Geneva Act (2015) extended the Lisbon system to GIs and opened it to organisations such as the EU. India is not a party.

Remember: Paris FALSE, Madrid DECEPTIVE, Lisbon REGISTER, TRIPS TWO TIERS.

slides.part: Chapter 14: The International Framework
slides.title: TRIPS Article 22: protection for every GI
slides.html:
Article 22 defines a GI and protects every GI, but only against uses that mislead the public or amount to unfair competition.

The TRIPS Agreement, Articles 22 to 24, sets the minimum standards. Article 22 gives the definition and the basic protection for all goods; Article 23 adds a stronger layer for wines and spirits; Article 24 sets the exceptions.

ProvisionContentExam note
Art. 22(1)GIs identify a good as originating in a member's territory, or a region or locality in it, where a given quality, reputation or other characteristic is essentially attributable to geographical origin.The core definition.
Art. 22(2)Members must provide legal means to prevent (a) misleading representation of origin and (b) acts of unfair competition (Article 10bis Paris).A misleading test applies to ordinary GIs.
Art. 22(3)Refuse or invalidate a trade mark containing a GI for goods not of that origin, where use would mislead as to true origin (ex officio if the law permits, or at an interested party's request).—
Art. 22(4)Protection against a GI literally true as to the territory of origin but falsely representing that the goods originate elsewhere.Covers misleading homonyms.

Notes reference: Table 19: TRIPS Articles 22 to 24 (the Article 22 rows; Articles 23 and 24 follow).

The key word is mislead. For an ordinary GI the claimant must show that the use misleads as to origin or is unfair competition. Keep this in mind: Article 23 removes exactly this requirement for wines and spirits.

slides.part: Chapter 14: The International Framework
slides.title: TRIPS Article 23: extra protection for wines and spirits
slides.html:
For wines and spirits Article 23 drops the misleading test, so the GI cannot be used on goods of other origin even with a true-origin label, translation or "type".

ProvisionContentExam note
Art. 23(1)Additional protection for wines and spirits: use is barred even where the true origin is indicated, the GI is translated, or it is accompanied by "kind", "type", "style", "imitation" and the like.Example: "Scotch like whisky" is not allowed. No need to prove that the public is misled.
Art. 23(2)Refusal or invalidation of trade marks for wines or spirits containing a GI identifying wines or spirits not of that origin.Applies regardless of whether the GI is registered and without a misleading test.
Art. 23(3)Homonymous GIs for wines: protection for each indication, with practical conditions to differentiate them and equitable treatment of producers.—
Art. 23(4)Negotiations on a multilateral system of notification and registration of GIs for wines.The international register has not yet been agreed.

This is why TRIPS is said to create two classes of GIs. Ordinary GIs are protected only against misleading use (Article 22). Wines and spirits are protected without any need to show that the public is misled (Article 23).

Remember: three Ts do not save the user of a wine or spirit GI: Truth (true origin stated), Translation, and Type words ("kind", "type", "style", "imitation").

Exam focus. India goes further. Section 22(3) of the GI Act mirrors Article 23 but can extend beyond wines and spirits, to any goods notified under Section 22(2) (chapter 15).

slides.part: Chapter 14: The International Framework
slides.title: TRIPS Article 24: the exceptions
slides.html:
Article 24 limits the GI shield: it preserves existing protection, saves long-standing or good faith users and trade marks, and excludes common terms.

ProvisionContentExam note
Art. 24(3)Members shall not diminish GI protection existing immediately before TRIPS.—
Art. 24(4)A member need not stop continued use of another member's GI for wines or spirits by its nationals who used it either for at least 10 years before 15 April 1994, or in good faith before that date.The two conditions are alternatives.
Art. 24(5)Trade marks applied for, registered or acquired through good faith use either before TRIPS applied in that member or before the GI was protected in its country of origin are not prejudiced.The trade mark "grandfather clause".
Art. 24(6)No obligation to protect a GI identical with the customary term in common language for the goods, or with the customary name of a grape variety.Common terms cannot be GIs.

Article 24 does three jobs. Article 24(3) is a standstill: no member may cut back the protection it already gave. Articles 24(4) and 24(5) look backwards and protect those who were there first. Article 24(6) keeps common words in common use.

Exam focus. In Art. 24(4) write "or", not "and". Ten years' use before 15 April 1994 is enough on its own, and so is good faith use before that date.

slides.part: Chapter 14: The International Framework
slides.title: The grandfather clause and the EC–US wine agreement
slides.html:
The "grandfather clause" means the Article 24(4) and 24(5) exceptions, and a prefix alone never makes a wine or spirit GI lawful on goods of other origin.

"Grandfather clause" refers to the exceptions in Articles 24(4) and 24(5), which let existing users and good faith trade marks continue.

Caveat. The classroom formula "prefixes + GI = allowed TM", illustrated by "Uncle Sam" + "Scotch Whisky", must be read with care: under Article 23(1) a prefix does not by itself make the use lawful, so "Uncle Sam Scotch Whisky" for whisky not from Scotland would ordinarily be barred. It can continue only if a grandfather exception applies, for example a mark registered or used in good faith before the relevant date.

So reason in this order:

  1. Is a wine or spirit GI being used on goods not of that origin? Then Article 23(1) bars the use, prefix or no prefix.
  2. Does a grandfather exception apply: Article 24(4) (at least 10 years' use before 15 April 1994, or good faith use before that date) or Article 24(5) (a good faith trade mark from before the relevant date)?
  3. If yes, the existing use or mark may continue; if not, it is barred.

Bilateral example: the 2006 Agreement between the European Community and the United States on trade in wine. The USA agreed to restrict certain "semi generic" names such as Champagne and Chablis to EU wines, while letting existing users with approved labels continue.

The deal follows the grandfather pattern: the names are restricted for the future, but those already using them with approved labels carry on.

slides.part: Chapter 15: The Geographical Indications of Goods (Registration and Protection) Act, 1999
slides.title: Background and the definitions in Section 2
slides.html:
India's GI Act, enacted after TRIPS, registers and protects GIs for goods, and Section 2 defines its four building blocks: GI, goods, indication and producer.

Enacted after India's ratification of TRIPS, the Geographical Indications of Goods (Registration and Protection) Act, 1999 provides for the registration and protection of GIs relating to goods. It came into force on 15 September 2003. The GI Registry is at Chennai. A uniform GI logo (introduced in 2018) is used across all GIs.

ProvisionContentKey words
Section 2(1)(e): geographical indicationAn indication identifying goods (agricultural, natural or manufactured) as originating or manufactured in a territory, region or locality, where a given quality, reputation or other characteristic is essentially attributable to geographical origin; and, for manufactured goods, where one of the activities of production, processing or preparation takes place there."Essentially attributable to its geographical origin". For manufactured goods, only one of production, processing or preparation need occur in the area.
Section 2(1)(f): goodsAny agricultural, natural or manufactured goods, or goods of handicraft or of industry, and includes foodstuff.Unlike TRIPS, the Act divides goods into categories.
Section 2(1)(g): indicationIncludes any name, geographical or figurative representation, or a combination, conveying or suggesting geographical origin.Geographical names need not be used: a non geographical name or a figurative sign can qualify.
Section 2(1)(k): producerFor agricultural goods, one who produces the goods (including one who processes or packages them); for natural goods, one who exploits them; for handicraft or industrial goods, one who makes or manufactures them; and any person who trades or deals in such production, exploitation, making or manufacture.Answers the question: whose interest must the applicant represent?

Notes reference: Table 20: Definitions in Section 2.

slides.part: Chapter 15: The Geographical Indications of Goods (Registration and Protection) Act, 1999
slides.title: The Register and the registration procedure
slides.html:
A body representing the producers registers the GI in Part A as proprietor, and the producers who actually use it then register in Part B as authorised users.

The Register (Sections 6 and 7) has two parts:

PartContentsWho
Part AThe registered GI and its registered proprietor.The association, organisation or authority that applied (proprietor).
Part BRegistered authorised users.Producers of the community who are registered (certified) to use the GI.

Notes reference: Table 21: Parts A and B of the Register.

Section 11(1). Any association of persons or producers, or any organisation or authority established by or under law, representing the interest of the producers of the goods, may apply to the Registrar in the prescribed form with the prescribed fee.

The procedure then runs in seven steps (the detail of what the application must contain comes later in this chapter):

  1. Application by a body representing the producers (Section 11), with the statement of case, map and particulars (Section 11(2) and Rule 32 of the GI Rules, 2002).
  2. Examination by the Registrar, who may consult a group of experts.
  3. Acceptance and advertisement in the GI Journal.
  4. Opposition by any person within the prescribed period, and decision.
  5. Registration in Part A; certificate issued.
  6. Producers apply to be registered as authorised users in Part B.
  7. Registration valid for ten years and renewable.

Notes reference: Figure 3: GI registration procedure.

slides.part: Chapter 15: The Geographical Indications of Goods (Registration and Protection) Act, 1999
slides.title: Who may apply: Toda embroidery and government bodies
slides.html:
Section 11(1) asks one question of every applicant, whether it represents the interest of the producers, and community bodies, NGOs and statutory boards can all qualify.

Toda embroidery GI (GI proceedings)

The Toda embroidery GI application was filed in 2008 by the Toda Nalavaazhvu Sangam (TNS) and the Keystone Foundation (KF), an NGO working in the Nilgiris, together with Poompuhar (the Tamil Nadu Handicrafts Development Corporation); the GI was registered in 2013.

After advertisement the issue arose whether TNS and KF represented the Toda community. It was held that they did. The legal point is Section 11(1): the applicant must represent the interest of the producers.

Government bodies as proprietors. Government bodies can be GI proprietors because Section 11(1) includes an authority established by or under law: for example the Tea Board (Darjeeling), the Coffee Board, the Spices Board and horticulture boards.

Both points answer the same question from different directions. An NGO is not itself a producer, but it may represent the producers. A public board qualifies because the Act expressly names an authority established by or under law. The harder case is a body that is also the only user, which is the Tirupati Laddu question.

slides.part: Chapter 15: The Geographical Indications of Goods (Registration and Protection) Act, 1999
slides.title: Tirupati Laddu: can a temple offering be a GI?
slides.html:
The Tirupati Laddu GI survived both challenges on procedure alone, so whether a temple offering held by one body can be a GI remains undecided.

Tirupati Laddu: can a divine offering connected solely with a temple be a GI?

  1. Tirumala Tirupati Devasthanams (TTD) applied on 31 March 2008 (Application No. 121, Class 30, foodstuffs); the GI was registered in September 2009.
  2. A public interest petition in the Madras High Court was dismissed in June 2010 because the alternative remedy of rectification under Section 27 was available.
  3. A rectification petition was then filed with the GI Registry. Its grounds: the laddu is a sacred offering (prasadam), not "goods" under Section 2(1)(f); registration in favour of a single entity defeats the collective purpose of GIs; and it offends Section 9(a) and (d).
  4. The Registry dismissed it on 30 July 2012 for want of locus standi (the petitioner was not a "person aggrieved" under Section 27(1)), with costs of Rs 10,000.

The merits question was never decided. Critics note that Part B of the Register lists no user other than TTD.

Exam focus. For "Critically examine the Tirupati Laddu GI", argue both sides. For the registration: Section 11(1) admits an authority established by or under law. Against it: the petitioners' grounds (not "goods", a single entity, Section 9(a) and (d)), clause (e) being linked in class to prasad, and a Part B with no other user.

slides.part: Chapter 15: The Geographical Indications of Goods (Registration and Protection) Act, 1999
slides.title: What cannot be a GI (Section 9) and homonymous GIs (Section 10)
slides.html:
Section 9 bars seven kinds of GI, from deceptive names to false homonyms, while Section 10 admits a genuine homonym if consumers will not be confused.

ClauseA GI shall not be registered ifExamples and notes
(a)its use would be likely to deceive or cause confusion.—
(b)its use would be contrary to any law for the time being in force.Classroom examples: mahua taadi (toddy), bhang thandai, Meghalaya bird feather cap. Relevant laws: state excise laws (liquor), the NDPS (Narcotic Drugs and Psychotropic Substances) Act, 1985 and state excise rules (bhang), and the Wildlife (Protection) Act, 1972 (feathers of protected birds).
(c)it comprises or contains scandalous or obscene matter.—
(d)it comprises or contains matter likely to hurt the religious susceptibilities of any class or section of citizens.Raised against the Tirupati Laddu.
(e)it would otherwise be disentitled to protection in a court.Linked in class to prasad (temple offerings).
(f)it is a generic name or indication, not or no longer protected in its country of origin, or fallen into disuse there.—
(g)although literally true as to the territory of origin, it falsely represents that the goods originate in another territory.The homonym problem; compare TRIPS Article 22(4).

Notes reference: Table 22: Section 9: prohibited GIs.

Remember: "Don't Let Sacred Rituals Offend Good Faith": Deceive, Law, Scandalous, Religious, Otherwise disentitled, Generic, False homonym, clauses (a) to (g).

Homonymous GIs: Section 10. A homonymous GI may be registered, subject to Section 7, if the Registrar is satisfied, after considering the practical conditions under which it will be differentiated from other homonymous indications and the need for equitable treatment of the producers, that consumers will not be confused or misled. Rule 32(6)(h) requires the applicant to state the differentiating factors and the protective measures adopted.

The two provisions work as a pair: Section 9(g) shuts out a homonym that falsely suggests another origin, while Section 10 lets in one that can be told apart (compare TRIPS Art. 23(3) for wines).

slides.part: Chapter 15: The Geographical Indications of Goods (Registration and Protection) Act, 1999
slides.title: What the application must contain
slides.html:
An application is a file of proof: how the place shapes the goods, the map and the producers, plus, under Rule 32(6), the benchmark and the quality mechanism.

Section 11 sets out what the application must state; Rule 32(6) of the GI Rules, 2002 adds the particulars that prove the link and the quality control:

ProvisionWhat must be stated or supplied
Section 11(2)(a)How the GI designates the goods as originating from the territory, in respect of specific quality, reputation or other characteristics due exclusively or essentially to the geographical environment, with its inherent natural and human factors, and where production, processing or preparation takes place.
Section 11(2)(b), (c)The class of goods; a geographical map of the territory.
Section 11(2)(d) to (f)The appearance of the GI (words, figurative elements or both); particulars of producers proposed to be registered initially; other prescribed particulars.
Section 11(3)A single application may cover several classes of goods, with a fee for each class.
Rule 32(6)(a)An affidavit on how the applicant represents the interest of the producers.
Rule 32(6)(b)The standards benchmark or industry standard for production, exploitation, making or manufacture, with a description of any human creativity involved.
Rule 32(6)(c)The mechanism to ensure that standards, quality, integrity and consistency are maintained by the producers.
Rule 32(6)(d), (e)Three certified copies of the map (with title, publisher and date of issue); the special human skill involved or the uniqueness of the geographical environment.
Rule 32(6)(f), (g)Full name and address of the applicant body; particulars of any inspection structure regulating use of the GI.
Rule 32(6)(h)For a homonymous GI, the differentiating factors and protective measures against confusion.

Notes reference: Table 23: Contents of a GI application.

Remember: Rule 32(6) runs A to H: Affidavit, Benchmark, Checks (quality mechanism), Diagrams (maps), Exceptional skill or environment, Full name and address, Guards (inspection structure), Homonym measures.

slides.part: Chapter 15: The Geographical Indications of Goods (Registration and Protection) Act, 1999
slides.title: Benchmarks, beneficiaries and how closely goods are checked
slides.html:
The benchmark must show a link to the place, not a standard met anywhere, and an Indian GI is checked only against the specifications stated in the application.

Classroom example on the benchmark (Rule 32(6)(b)): a GI sought by Reliance for petroleum products: ISO standards cannot be the benchmark. The benchmark must show qualities attributable to geographical origin, and a general industry standard that can be met anywhere does not show that link.

Basmati rice: the Indian Basmati GI, held by APEDA (Agricultural and Processed Food Products Export Development Authority), was contested over whether districts of Madhya Pradesh should be included in the GI area; the case illustrates the importance of defining the area and the quality mechanism (Rule 32(6)(c)).

Who benefits, and how closely goods are scrutinised:

  1. Proprietors are not direct beneficiaries. They are the channel through which the benefit percolates into the community; the producers who use the GI benefit.
  2. The proprietor is not, as such, responsible for maintaining quality, although Rule 32(6)(c) and (g) require a quality mechanism and any inspection structure to be described.
  3. India: GI goods are scrutinised only on the specifications in the application; the cultivation process usually does not matter (organic or chemical farming of Basmati; natural or synthetic dyes for Pattachitra).
  4. European Union: the entire process from the start is considered (for cheese, milk quality and cow fodder). An Indian GI therefore guarantees less about how the product was made than an EU PDO.

Exam focus. This slide is the core of "Does Indian GI law protect quality, or only origin?". Quality enters through the Rule 32 benchmark and mechanism, but only as far as the stated specifications go.

slides.part: Chapter 15: The Geographical Indications of Goods (Registration and Protection) Act, 1999
slides.title: Rights conferred by registration
slides.html:
Registration is the gateway: without it there is no infringement action, and with it the proprietor and authorised users can sue, but the right cannot be assigned or licensed.

Chapter IV of the Act sets out what registration gives:

SectionContent
Section 20No action lies for infringement of an unregistered GI (subsection (1)); rights of action for passing off are preserved (subsection (2)).
Section 21A valid registration gives the registered proprietor and authorised users the right to obtain relief for infringement, and gives the authorised user the exclusive right to use the GI for the registered goods, subject to registered conditions. Where several authorised users hold identical or similar GIs, none gets an exclusive right against the others.
Section 23Registration is prima facie evidence of validity.
Section 24A GI right is not assignable or transferable: an authorised user's right cannot be assigned, transmitted, licensed, pledged or mortgaged, but on the authorised user's death it devolves on the successor in title.

Notes reference: Table 24: Rights conferred by registration.

Two points follow. First, an unregistered GI is not worthless, because Section 20(2) keeps passing off available. Second, the exclusive right to use is given to the authorised user, the producer who actually uses the GI; and because the GI is a community right, Section 24 stops that right being sold or licensed.

Exam focus. Short answer on Section 20: state both halves (no infringement action for an unregistered GI; passing off preserved), then contrast Section 21 and Section 23.

slides.part: Chapter 15: The Geographical Indications of Goods (Registration and Protection) Act, 1999
slides.title: Infringement: Section 22
slides.html:
A person who is not an authorised user infringes by misleading use, unfair competition or a false homonym, and notified goods get Article 23-style protection under Section 22(3).

A person who is not an authorised user infringes a registered GI if he:

  1. (a) uses the GI in the designation or presentation of goods so as to indicate or suggest that they originate in an area other than their true place of origin, in a way that misleads as to geographical origin;
  2. (b) uses a GI in a way that constitutes unfair competition, including passing off. Explanation 1: unfair competition is any act contrary to honest practices in industrial or commercial matters. Explanation 2 deems unfair: acts creating confusion with a competitor's establishment, goods or activities; false allegations discrediting a competitor; and uses of GIs liable to mislead as to the nature, manufacturing process, characteristics, suitability or quantity of goods;
  3. (c) uses another GI that is literally true as to origin but falsely represents that the goods come from the area of the registered GI ("same place, same product, one GI, one non GI").

Section 22(3) gives additional protection to goods notified under Section 22(2): use of another GI on such goods infringes even when the true origin is indicated, when it is used in translation, or with words like "kind", "style" or "imitation", for example "Kolhapuri style chappal" or "Banarasi type silk". This mirrors TRIPS Article 23 but can extend beyond wines and spirits; it applies only to notified goods.

Section 22(4): further dealings, including processing or packaging, in goods lawfully acquired from an authorised user do not infringe, unless the condition of the goods is impaired after they are put on the market.

Exam focus. In a problem, "type" or "style" is caught automatically only if the goods are notified under Section 22(2). Otherwise argue Section 22(1): the use misleads as to origin, or is unfair competition.

slides.part: Chapter 15: The Geographical Indications of Goods (Registration and Protection) Act, 1999
slides.title: Trade marks and prior users: Sections 25 and 26
slides.html:
Chapter V settles clashes with trade marks: misleading marks and marks containing GIs of notified goods are refused, but earlier good faith marks, common names and own names are saved.

ProvisionRuleCompare (TRIPS)
Section 25The Registrar of Trade Marks shall, suo motu or at the request of an interested party, refuse or invalidate a trade mark that (a) contains or consists of a GI for goods not originating in the territory indicated, where use would confuse or mislead as to true origin, or (b) contains or consists of a GI identifying goods notified under Section 22(2).Art. 22(3) for (a); Art. 23(2) for (b)
Section 26(1)A trade mark containing a GI that was applied for or registered in good faith, or acquired through good faith use, either (a) before the commencement of the Act or (b) before the date of filing of the GI application, is not prejudiced.Art. 24(5), the grandfather clause
Section 26(2)The Act does not apply to a GI identical with the term customary in common language as the common name of the goods in any part of India on or before 1 January 1995.Art. 24(6), common terms
Section 26(3)A person may use his own name or his predecessor's name in business, unless used so as to confuse or mislead.—

Section 26(1) works like the Art. 24(5) grandfather clause. It is what saved ITC: its use of "Darjeeling Lounge" began in good faith before the Act came into force (Section 26(1)(a)).

slides.part: Chapter 15: The Geographical Indications of Goods (Registration and Protection) Act, 1999
slides.title: The five-year limitation: Section 26(4)
slides.html:
No action lies against a trade mark five years after the earlier of knowledge or the mark's published registration, provided the GI is not used or registered in bad faith.

Section 26(4), limitation period (very important): no action in connection with the use or registration of a trade mark can be taken after five years from the date on which the infringing use or registration became known to the registered proprietor or authorised user, or after the date of registration of the trade mark (if published by then), if that date is earlier than the date of knowledge, provided the GI is not used or registered in bad faith.

Compute it in four steps:

  1. Identify the two possible starting points: (i) the date the infringing use or registration became known to the GI proprietor or authorised user; (ii) the date of registration of the trade mark, if published by then.
  2. If the registration date is earlier than the date of knowledge, the five years run from registration; otherwise from the date of knowledge.
  3. Check the bad faith condition: the bar applies only where "such geographical indication is not used or registered in bad faith".
  4. After five years, and without bad faith, no action can be taken against the trade mark.

Notes reference: Figure 4: Computing the Section 26(4) limitation.

Applied: Tea Board v. ITC

ITC's "Darjeeling Lounge" had been in use since 2003 and the Tea Board sued in 2010. The Calcutta High Court held the claim barred by the five year limitation in Section 26(4).

Exam focus. The common slip is to count only from knowledge. Always check whether the trade mark was registered (and published) earlier, because then the five years run from registration.

slides.part: Chapter 15: The Geographical Indications of Goods (Registration and Protection) Act, 1999
slides.title: Tea Board, India v. ITC Limited (Darjeeling Lounge)
slides.html:
The first Indian decision on infringement of a registered GI went against the proprietor: the claim was time-barred, and ITC's pre-Act good faith use was protected.

Tea Board, India v. ITC Limited ("Darjeeling Lounge")

Citation
C.S. No. 250 of 2010, Calcutta High Court. Interim injunction refused on 20 April 2011; appeal dismissed by a Division Bench on 24 August 2011, 2011 (48) PTC 169 (Cal); the Supreme Court remitted the matter for expeditious disposal on 22 January 2016; final judgment by Sahidullah Munshi J. on 4 February 2019.
Facts
ITC named a lounge at its ITC Sonar hotel in Kolkata the "Darjeeling Lounge", in use since 1 January 2003. The Tea Board, registered proprietor of the Darjeeling GI and certification marks, objected: in 2005 it reportedly issued a notice not to use the name and opposed ITC's trade mark application, and further letters followed in 2006 and 2008. It sued in 2010 for infringement of the GI and certification marks, passing off and dilution.
Issues
Whether naming a lounge "Darjeeling" infringed the GI or certification marks; whether the claim was barred by Section 26(4); whether passing off or unfair competition was made out.
Holding
Interim relief was refused at both levels in 2011. The suit was dismissed in 2019: the claim was barred by the five year limitation in Section 26(4), since the name had been used since 2003 and the suit was filed in 2010; and Section 26(1)(a) protected use begun in good faith before the Act came into force in September 2003. ITC could continue using the name.
Significance
The first decision on infringement of a registered GI in India. It shows the limits of GI protection (goods, not services), the force of Section 26(4) and the protection of prior good faith use.

Notes reference: Table 25: Case brief: Tea Board, India v. ITC Limited.

slides.part: Chapter 15: The Geographical Indications of Goods (Registration and Protection) Act, 1999
slides.title: Scotch Whisky and Champagne: foreign GIs in Indian courts
slides.html:
Foreign GIs are enforced in India: Scotch Whisky against "type" and "style" uses, and Champagne even against non-alcoholic drinks.

Scotch Whisky cases

The Scotch Whisky Association has brought several actions in India against Indian whisky makers using "Scotch" or Scottish imagery. They illustrate the protection of a spirits GI against use on goods of other origin, including with words such as "type" or "style" (TRIPS Article 23; Section 22(3)).

Comité Interprofessionnel du Vin de Champagne v. Chinar Agro Fruit Products (Champagne case)

Citation
CS(COMM) 1194/2016, Delhi High Court, Sanjeev Sachdeva J., 7 September 2017; 2017 SCC OnLine Del 10704.
Facts
The French body that protects the Champagne appellation holds a registered GI for Champagne in India. The defendant made fruit beer, fruit juice, soft drinks and non alcoholic sparkling drinks and sold some under the name CHAMPAGNE in Delhi, Punjab and Jammu and Kashmir. It did not appear and was proceeded against ex parte.
Issue
Whether use of CHAMPAGNE for non alcoholic beverages not from Champagne infringed the registered GI.
Holding
Permanent injunction granted.
Significance
A registered foreign GI is protected in India even against use on different goods, where the use misleads or trades on the GI's reputation.

Notes reference: Table 26: Case brief: Champagne v. Chinar Agro Fruit Products.

slides.part: Chapter 15: The Geographical Indications of Goods (Registration and Protection) Act, 1999
slides.title: Bikaneri Bhujia: how a registered user presents its goods
slides.html:
Even a registered authorised user may have to present its goods distinctly: the Delhi High Court ordered alternative packaging in the Bikaneri Bhujia dispute.

Bikaji Foods International Ltd. v. Desai Brothers Ltd. (Bikaneri Bhujia case, 2023)

Decided by the Delhi High Court on 11 October 2023, together with Bikaner Bhujia Udyog Sangh v. Desai Brothers Ltd. The dispute concerned alleged unauthorised use of the GI "Bikaneri Bhujia" (Application No. 142, Class 30, proprietor Bikaner Bhujia Udhyog Sangh).

The Court directed the defendants to adopt alternative packaging so that their products would be distinguishable. Desai Brothers is itself a registered authorised user of the GI, so the case concerns how a registered user presents its goods.

Read it with Section 21: where several authorised users hold identical or similar GIs, none gets an exclusive right against the others. So the dispute was about presentation, not about the right to use the name.

Latest: in Unibic Foods India Pvt. Ltd. v. Bikaner Bhujia Udyog Sangh (Delhi High Court, C. Hari Shankar J., 18 March 2026) the appeals were disposed of on terms that included the appellant's undertaking not to challenge the Bikaneri Bhujia GI registration in any forum.

slides.part: Chapter 15: The Geographical Indications of Goods (Registration and Protection) Act, 1999
slides.title: Prada and the Kolhapuri chappal (2025)
slides.html:
The Prada episode shows two limits of GI law: only registered proprietors and authorised users can sue, and a GI protects a name, not a design.

  1. In June 2025 Prada showed, in its Spring/Summer 2026 men's collection in Milan, toe ring sandals closely resembling Kolhapuri chappals, described simply as leather sandals and priced at about Rs 1.2 lakh. After criticism, including a complaint by the Maharashtra Chamber of Commerce, Industry and Agriculture, Prada acknowledged the Indian inspiration.
  2. A PIL (public interest litigation) by six advocates in the Bombay High Court sought restraint, compensation for artisans and a public apology. On 16 July 2025 a Bench of Chief Justice Alok Aradhe and Sandeep V. Marne J. dismissed it as not maintainable.
  3. The reason: the registered proprietors, LIDCOM (Sant Rohidas Leather Industries and Charmakar Development Corporation, Maharashtra) and LIDKAR (Dr. Babu Jagjivan Ram Leather Industries Development Corporation, Karnataka), hold the rights under Section 21 and can sue for infringement; an action that a registered proprietor can bring by suit cannot be pursued through a PIL. The Court did not examine whether the products were similar.
  4. In December 2025 Prada signed a memorandum of understanding with LIDCOM and LIDKAR for a "Prada Made in India, Inspired by Kolhapuri Chappals" project.

Lessons: standing belongs to the registered proprietor and authorised users; and a GI protects the indication (the name "Kolhapuri"), not a design, so copying the look of a product without using the name may fall outside GI infringement.

slides.part: Chapter 15: The Geographical Indications of Goods (Registration and Protection) Act, 1999
slides.title: Remedies and appeals
slides.html:
Infringement suits are filed in a District Court or higher, and since the Intellectual Property Appellate Board was abolished in 2021, rectification lies before the Registrar or the High Court.

Infringement suits are filed in a District Court or higher.

Law update. The Intellectual Property Appellate Board (IPAB), which heard appeals and rectification matters under the Act, was abolished by the Tribunals Reforms Act, 2021; rectification now lies before the Registrar or the High Court.

Putting the chapter's enforcement rules together:

QuestionAnswerAuthority
Is the GI registered?If not, no infringement action; passing off remainsSection 20
Who can sue?The registered proprietor and authorised users, not PIL petitionersSection 21; Prada PIL
Where?A District Court or higher—
What is infringement?Misleading use, unfair competition, false homonyms; extra protection for notified goodsSection 22
Is a claim against a trade mark time-barred?After five years from knowledge, or from earlier published registrationSection 26(4); Tea Board v. ITC
Who may seek rectification?A "person aggrieved", now before the Registrar or the High CourtSection 27(1); Tirupati Laddu

slides.part: Chapter 16: GI Protection in the European Union and the United States
slides.title: The EU framework
slides.html:
The EU began with quality schemes for agricultural products and foodstuffs, and today one Regulation covers agricultural products, wine and spirits while another covers craft and industrial products.

The EU first protected GIs through quality schemes for agricultural products and foodstuffs (PDO and PGI) and separate schemes for wines, spirit drinks and aromatised wines; recently craft and industrial products such as handlooms were added. Different member states have different GI products, all recognised at EU level by regulation.

  1. Regulation (EU) 2024/1143 (adopted April 2024) now governs GIs for wine, spirit drinks and agricultural products, replacing Regulation (EU) No 1151/2012.
  2. Regulation (EU) 2023/2411 (18 October 2023; in force 16 November 2023; applicable from 1 December 2025) protects craft and industrial products, with applications handled by the EUIPO (European Union Intellectual Property Office). Examples: Carrara marble, Limoges porcelain, Murano glass.
  3. PDO and PGI are both available for agricultural products, foodstuffs and wines; spirit drinks and aromatised wine products use the label "geographical indication". The difference between PDO and PGI is the strength of the link to the area, not the type of product.

Law update. Older materials cite Regulation (EU) No 1151/2012, which Regulation (EU) 2024/1143 has replaced. Craft and industrial GIs are protected EU-wide only from 1 December 2025.

slides.part: Chapter 16: GI Protection in the European Union and the United States
slides.title: PDO and PGI
slides.html:
A PDO needs every production step in the area and qualities essentially or exclusively due to it, while a PGI needs only one step there.

FeaturePDO (protected designation of origin)PGI (protected geographical indication)
DefinitionThe name of a region or specific place used for an agricultural product or foodstuff originating there, whose quality or characteristics are essentially or exclusively due to the area, and whose production and processing all take place there.A product whose final production, processing or preparation (at least one step) takes place in the defined area, and whose quality, reputation or characteristic is attributable to it.
ExampleShetland Lamb PDO: area confined to the Shetland Islands.Scotch Beef PGI: area not precisely defined, including most of Scotland. Westfälischer Knochenschinken PGI ham: produced in Westphalia using age old techniques, though the meat can come from anywhere.
Animals (lamb and beef examples)Reared for their entire lives, slaughtered and dressed in the designated area.The same rule is recorded for Scotch Beef; the distinction lies in how the area is defined.

Notes reference: Table 27: PDO and PGI.

Roquefort (PDO): cheese made from sheep's milk, ripened with the mould Penicillium roqueforti in the natural caves of Roquefort.

Correction. The mould is generally described as aerobic though tolerant of low oxygen, and the caves are known for natural air circulation through rock fissures, so "anaerobic conditions of caves" is doubtful.

GI for wines and aromatised drinks: a name identifying the product as originating in a country, region or locality where a given quality, reputation or other characteristic is essentially attributable to that origin.

slides.part: Chapter 16: GI Protection in the European Union and the United States
slides.title: Handicraft GIs and single producers
slides.html:
EU-wide protection for handicrafts arrived only with Regulation (EU) 2023/2411, which normally needs a producer group but lets a single producer apply by exception.

EU wide protection for handicrafts came with Regulation (EU) 2023/2411 (applicable from 1 December 2025); the earlier Regulation (EC) No 510/2006 dealt with agricultural products and foodstuffs (some non food agricultural products were listed in its annex) and did not create a general handicraft system.

Under the 2023 Regulation the applicant is normally a producer group, but a single producer may apply by way of exception, on meeting cumulative conditions (Article 8(2)); the GI then relates to the village or area to which that producer belongs.

Two contrasts with India are worth making. India's definition of goods in Section 2(1)(f) already includes goods of handicraft, as with Toda embroidery and Kolhapuri chappals. And the single-entity objection raised against the Tirupati Laddu has an EU answer: one producer may hold a craft GI, but only as an exception on cumulative conditions.

slides.part: Chapter 16: GI Protection in the European Union and the United States
slides.title: The United States: GIs through trade mark law
slides.html:
The USA recognises GIs through trade marks, certification marks and collective marks, treating a GI as private property rather than an entry on a public register.

The USA recognises GIs through trade marks, certification marks and collective marks. A certification mark certifies that goods meet stated standards, including regional origin, and its owner (often a public body) may not itself produce the goods; DARJEELING, registered by the Tea Board, is an example. The US treats a GI as private property enforced under trade mark law, in contrast with the EU's public register.

slides.part: Chapter 16: GI Protection in the European Union and the United States
slides.title: Sustainability in EU GI law
slides.html:
Regulation (EU) 2024/1143 brings environmental, social and economic sustainability into EU GIs, through product specifications and producer-group sustainability reports.

Regulation (EU) 2024/1143 brings sustainability (environmental, social and economic) into the GI system: producers may agree sustainable practices that are written into the product specification, and producer groups may prepare sustainability reports.

Caveat. In class it was said that an applicant has to show sustainability when filing; check the exact wording of the Regulation before stating that this is mandatory for every applicant.

Note the words "may agree" and "may prepare" in the notes' account of the Regulation; that is why the class statement needs checking. The wider point holds: the EU looks further into how a product is made, widening the gap with India, where scrutiny stops at the specifications in the application.

slides.part: Quick revision
slides.title: Part D in one page
slides.html:
A GI links goods to a place whose qualities or reputation they carry, and four treaties and three systems protect that link in different ways.

  1. A GI links goods to a place whose qualities or reputation they carry. Every appellation of origin is a GI, and every GI is an indication of source, but not the other way round.
  2. Paris (1883) protected indications of source against false use; Madrid (1891) added deceptive use; Lisbon (1958) created an international register for appellations of origin.
  3. TRIPS Articles 22 to 24 set minimum standards, with stronger protection for wines and spirits and grandfather exceptions.
  4. India's GI Act, 1999 (in force 2003; Registry at Chennai) registers GIs for goods in Part A and authorised users in Part B, and bars registration on the grounds in Section 9.
  5. It protects only registered GIs (Section 20), defines infringement in Section 22, and protects good faith trade marks with a five year limitation (Section 26(4), applied in Tea Board v. ITC).
  6. The EU uses PDO and PGI under Regulation (EU) 2024/1143 and, since 1 December 2025, craft and industrial GIs under Regulation (EU) 2023/2411; the US uses certification and collective marks.

slides.part: Practice questions
slides.title: Practice questions
slides.html:
1. Short answer: Distinguish an indication of source, a GI and an appellation of origin.
  2. Short answer: What is the effect of Section 20 of the GI Act?
  3. Short answer: State the grounds on which a GI cannot be registered under Section 9.
  4. Short answer: Explain the Section 26(4) limitation period.
  5. Short answer: What did the Court of Justice decide in the Parmesan case?
  6. Analytical: "TRIPS creates two classes of GIs." Discuss Articles 22 and 23 and the exceptions in Article 24.
  7. Analytical: Does Indian GI law protect quality, or only origin? Discuss with reference to Rule 32 and EU product specifications.
  8. Analytical: Critically examine the Tirupati Laddu GI.
  9. Problem: A Delhi company sells non alcoholic fizzy apple drinks labelled "Champagne style refresher". Another sells cotton saris made in Surat as "Banarasi type sarees". The registered proprietor of the Banarasi GI and the Champagne body wish to sue. Advise them.

slides.part: Answer plans
slides.title: Short answers: Q1 to Q3
slides.html:
Short answers score by defining first, then setting out the elements in the notes' order, each with its example or authority.

Q1. Distinguish an indication of source, a GI and an appellation of origin.

  1. Define a GI from TRIPS Art. 22(1) or Section 2(1)(e): a quality, reputation or other characteristic essentially attributable to geographical origin.
  2. Draw the three concentric circles: indication of source (outer; only the fact of making, "Made in India"); GI (middle; Darjeeling tea); appellation of origin (inner; raw materials, process, labour and skill from the place).
  3. Place each in the instruments: Paris Article 1(2) first used "indications of source" and "appellations of origin"; Lisbon (1958) adopted the French definition of an appellation; TRIPS defines the GI.
  4. Conclude with the nesting rule: every AO is a GI and every GI is an indication of source, but not the other way round.

Q2. What is the effect of Section 20 of the GI Act?

  1. State the rule: no action lies for infringement of an unregistered GI (Section 20(1)).
  2. State the saving: rights of action for passing off are preserved (Section 20(2)).
  3. Contrast registration: Section 21 gives the registered proprietor and authorised users the right to obtain relief for infringement; Section 23 makes registration prima facie evidence of validity.
  4. Illustrate standing with the Prada PIL: only the registered proprietors (LIDCOM, LIDKAR) and authorised users could sue.
  5. Conclude: registration is the gateway to the statutory action; without it, only passing off remains.

Q3. State the grounds on which a GI cannot be registered under Section 9.

  1. Introduce Section 9: "A GI shall not be registered if…"
  2. List clauses (a) to (g) in order: deceive or confuse; contrary to law; scandalous or obscene; hurts religious susceptibilities; otherwise disentitled to protection in a court; generic, not or no longer protected at home, or disused; literally true but falsely representing another origin.
  3. Add the notes' examples: mahua taadi, bhang thandai and the Meghalaya bird feather cap for (b) (excise laws, NDPS Act, Wildlife (Protection) Act, 1972); (d) raised against the Tirupati Laddu; (e) linked to prasad.
  4. Link (g) with TRIPS Art. 22(4) and with Section 10, which admits a homonym if consumers will not be confused.

slides.part: Answer plans
slides.title: Short answers: Q4 and Q5
slides.html:
For the limitation give the rule, the computation and an application, and for the Parmesan case give facts, issue, holding and the exam trap.

Q4. Explain the Section 26(4) limitation period.

  1. State the rule: no action in connection with the use or registration of a trade mark after five years.
  2. Identify the two starting points: the date the infringing use or registration became known to the registered proprietor or authorised user; the date of registration of the trade mark, if published by then.
  3. Compute: if registration is earlier than knowledge, time runs from registration; otherwise from knowledge.
  4. State the proviso: the bar applies only where the GI is not used or registered in bad faith.
  5. Apply Tea Board v. ITC: use since 2003, suit filed 2010, claim barred; add Section 26(1)(a), which protected good faith use begun before the Act.
  6. Conclude: a GI proprietor must act within five years against a conflicting trade mark.

Q5. What did the Court of Justice decide in the Parmesan case?

  1. Cite: Commission v. Germany, Case C 132/05, Court of Justice (Grand Chamber), 26 February 2008; Italy and the Czech Republic for the Commission, Denmark and Austria for Germany.
  2. Facts: cheese not made to the PDO specification sold in Germany as "Parmesan"; the Commission's translation argument.
  3. Issue: does "Parmesan" infringe the PDO "Parmigiano Reggiano", and did Germany have to act of its own motion?
  4. Holding: evocation, so translation is irrelevant; not shown to be generic; but the action was dismissed because the Commission did not prove that German law failed to protect the PDO.
  5. Conclude with the exam tip: the question is whether "Parmesan" infringes the PDO, not whether "parma cheese" violates "parmesan cheese".

slides.part: Answer plans
slides.title: Analytical answers: Q6 and Q7
slides.html:
Analytical answers need a thesis: TRIPS gives two levels of protection, and Indian law protects quality only as far as the stated specifications go.

Q6. "TRIPS creates two classes of GIs." Discuss Articles 22 and 23 and the exceptions in Article 24.

  1. Introduce: TRIPS Articles 22 to 24 set minimum standards; explain what "two classes" means.
  2. Article 22, all GIs: definition (Art. 22(1)); legal means against misleading representation and unfair competition (Art. 22(2)); trade marks refused where misleading (Art. 22(3)); misleading homonyms (Art. 22(4)). Stress the misleading test.
  3. Article 23, wines and spirits: barred even with the true origin, a translation or "kind", "type", "style", "imitation" ("Scotch like whisky"), with no need to prove the public is misled (Art. 23(1)); trade marks (Art. 23(2)); homonymous wine GIs (Art. 23(3)); the register not yet agreed (Art. 23(4)).
  4. Article 24: no diminishing of existing protection (Art. 24(3)); continued use for 10 years before 15 April 1994 or in good faith (Art. 24(4)); good faith trade marks (Art. 24(5)); customary terms and grape varieties (Art. 24(6)).
  5. Evaluate: "Uncle Sam" + "Scotch Whisky" is not saved by the prefix (Article 23(1)) but only by a grandfather exception; the 2006 EC–US wine agreement restricted "semi generic" names bilaterally.
  6. Conclude with India: Section 22(3) mirrors Article 23 but can extend beyond wines and spirits to notified goods.

Q7. Does Indian GI law protect quality, or only origin? Discuss with reference to Rule 32 and EU product specifications.

  1. Start from the definition: Section 2(1)(e) requires a quality, reputation or other characteristic essentially attributable to geographical origin.
  2. Show the quality hooks in Rule 32(6): (b) the standards benchmark (Reliance: ISO standards cannot be the benchmark); (c) the quality mechanism (Basmati and the Madhya Pradesh districts); (g) any inspection structure.
  3. Show the limits: the proprietor is not, as such, responsible for maintaining quality; scrutiny is only on the specifications; the cultivation process usually does not matter (Basmati farming; Pattachitra dyes).
  4. Contrast the EU: the entire process from the start (milk quality, cow fodder); a PDO needs all production and processing in the area; sustainability under Regulation (EU) 2024/1143, with the class caveat.
  5. Conclude: Indian law protects origin and the stated specifications, so an Indian GI guarantees less about how the product was made than an EU PDO.

slides.part: Answer plans
slides.title: Q8 (Tirupati Laddu) and Q9 (the problem)
slides.html:
For Tirupati weigh both sides of an undecided question, and for the problem run issues, rules, application and conclusion for each plaintiff.

Q8. Critically examine the Tirupati Laddu GI.

  1. Facts: TTD applied on 31 March 2008 (Application No. 121, Class 30, foodstuffs); registered September 2009.
  2. Procedure: Madras High Court PIL dismissed in June 2010 (alternative remedy of rectification under Section 27); rectification dismissed on 30 July 2012 for want of locus standi (not a "person aggrieved", Section 27(1)), costs Rs 10,000.
  3. Against the GI: a sacred offering is not "goods" (Section 2(1)(f)); a single entity defeats the collective purpose; Section 9(a) and (d), with (e) linked to prasad; Part B lists no user other than TTD.
  4. For the GI: Section 11(1) admits an authority established by or under law, as with the Tea Board; "goods" includes foodstuff.
  5. Compare the EU: a single producer may hold a craft GI only by exception (Article 8(2) of Regulation (EU) 2023/2411).
  6. Conclude: the merits were never decided, so the registration stands on procedure, not principle.

Q9. Problem: "Champagne style refresher" and "Banarasi type sarees".

  1. Issues: infringement of registered GIs; the effect of "style" and "type"; standing.
  2. Rules: Sections 20, 21 and 22 (with Explanations and subsections (2) and (3)) of the GI Act; TRIPS Articles 22 and 23; Champagne v. Chinar Agro; the Prada PIL (standing of proprietors).
  3. Application (standing): both plaintiffs are registered proprietors with standing.
  4. Application (Banarasi): "Banarasi type" misleads as to origin and may be unfair competition under Section 22(1); Section 22(3) catches "type" only if saris are notified under Section 22(2).
  5. Application (Champagne): Section 22(1) and the Chinar Agro decision support relief even for different goods; Section 22(3) again depends on notification.
  6. Conclusion: strong cases under Section 22(1); additional protection under Section 22(3) depends on notification.

slides.part: Chapter 18: Protection of Semiconductor Integrated Circuit Layout Designs
slides.title: What a layout design is
slides.html:
A layout design, or topography, is the three dimensional arrangement of a chip's elements and connections; it is fixed in masks, hence the US term "mask work".

Start with the science, because the law protects something very specific. An integrated circuit is a set of electronic components, chiefly transistors, with the conductive connections between them, formed in and on a thin piece of semiconductor material such as silicon.

The layout design or topography is the three dimensional disposition of the spatial patterns of those elements and connections in the layers of the chip. It is what defines the structure of the circuit.

The layout is fixed in the masks used to pattern each layer during manufacture. That is why United States law calls it a "mask work".

Integrated circuit

Components (chiefly transistors) and their connections, formed in and on a thin piece of semiconductor such as silicon.

Layout design or topography

The 3D arrangement of those elements and connections, layer by layer: the structure of the circuit.

Mask work

The US name for the same thing, because the layout is fixed in the masks.

Exam focus. Three names, one object: "topography" (EU), "mask work" (US) and "layout design" (TRIPS and India). Open a chip-law answer with this plain meaning, then give the statutory definition in Section 2(h) of the SICLD Act.

slides.part: Chapter 18: Protection of Semiconductor Integrated Circuit Layout Designs
slides.title: Moore's Law and chip piracy
slides.html:
Chips pack ever more transistors and take many years to design, yet a layout is easy to copy: that mismatch is why the law steps in.

Moore's Law is the observation by Gordon Moore (1965, revised in 1975) that the number of transistors on an integrated circuit doubles about every two years.

Exam focus. Moore's Law concerns transistors per chip, not the number of chips, although ever smaller and cheaper computers followed from it.

Chip piracy: the fruit of 15 to 20 years of research and development can be pirated and sold at low prices. Why? Because copying is comparatively easy:

  1. a competitor strips a chip layer by layer;
  2. photographs each layer; and
  3. reproduces the masks, and with them the layout.

Put the two ideas together. Design effort keeps rising, while copying stays cheap, so without protection the copier gets the benefit of the designer's investment. That is the policy problem a layout-design law answers.

slides.part: Chapter 18: Protection of Semiconductor Integrated Circuit Layout Designs
slides.title: Why a sui generis law
slides.html:
Neither copyright nor patent fits chip layouts, so countries created a sui generis right: a system of protection of its own kind.

A sui generis system is protection of its own kind, outside the usual categories of intellectual property. Chip layouts needed one because both existing regimes fail them, each for a different reason.

  1. Copyright cannot protect functional aspects, and the arrangement of a circuit is largely dictated by function. The valuable part of the layout would fall outside copyright.
  2. Patent law cannot protect mere rearrangement: most new layouts are improved arrangements of known elements that would fail the inventive step test.
  3. In India, Section 3(o) of the Patents Act, 1970 expressly excludes a topography of integrated circuits from patentability.
