Exam focus. "Why do copyright and patent law fit layout designs poorly?" is a set question. Give one reason for each regime, cite Section 3(o), and conclude that a sui generis right was needed.

slides.part: Chapter 18: Protection of Semiconductor Integrated Circuit Layout Designs
slides.title: The United States: CHIPS Act and SCPA
slides.html:
The US led chip law with the SCPA of 1984, a ten year sui generis right in mask works; the CHIPS Act of 2022 is industrial policy, not IP.

CHIPS and Science Act, 2022: provides large subsidies and tax credits to boost domestic semiconductor manufacturing and research and to compete internationally, mainly with East Asian producers. It is industrial policy, not intellectual property law, so it is not a source of layout-design rights.

Background reading: the book Chip War (Chris Miller, 2022) traces the history and geopolitics of the semiconductor industry.

The Semiconductor Chip Protection Act of 1984 (SCPA) (title 17, United States Code, sections 901 to 914) created a new kind of sui generis right in "mask works". It is a hybrid that combines features of three bodies of law:

From patent law

Registration.

From copyright law

Originality and a right against copying.

From competition policy

A reverse engineering exception.

Protection lasts ten years.

Remember: SCPA = P + C + C: patent (registration), copyright (originality, right against copying), competition (reverse engineering).

slides.part: Chapter 18: Protection of Semiconductor Integrated Circuit Layout Designs
slides.title: SCPA Section 906(a): reverse engineering
slides.html:
Section 906(a) lets anyone reproduce a mask work to study it, and then use what they learn in their own original mask work.

Section 906(a), SCPA. Permits reproduction of a mask work solely for teaching, analysing or evaluating the concepts or techniques embodied in it, and permits a person who does so to incorporate the results in an original mask work made for distribution.

The section has two limbs, and they work in sequence:

  1. Reproduce the mask work, but solely for teaching, analysing or evaluating its concepts or techniques.
  2. Incorporate the results of that study in an original mask work made for distribution.

This is the competition-policy part of the SCPA's hybrid. Competitors may learn the concepts and techniques, and build on them, but the end product must be their own original mask work. Simply copying a layout to sell it is not study and does not produce an original work, so it falls outside the exception.

Exam focus. A set question asks what Section 906(a) permits and what its Indian counterpart is. Answer: Section 18(3) of the SICLD Act, India's reverse engineering exception (see the Indian Act below).

slides.part: Chapter 18: Protection of Semiconductor Integrated Circuit Layout Designs
slides.title: The EU: Directive 87/54/EEC
slides.html:
The EU followed the US: member states must protect chip topographies that are their creator's own intellectual effort and not commonplace, protecting the topography, not the chip.

Council Directive 87/54/EEC of 16 December 1986 on the legal protection of topographies of semiconductor products requires member states to protect topographies that meet two conditions:

  1. they result from their creator's own intellectual effort; and
  2. they are not commonplace in the industry.

It protects the topography, not the microchip itself. The right is in the design pattern, so the chip as a physical product is not what is protected.

Notice the family resemblance. India's test of originality in Section 7(2) of the SICLD Act has the same two limbs: the creator's own intellectual efforts, and a design not commonly known to the trade at the time of creation.

Exam focus. In the essay question, the Directive (1986) is the second step in the "legislative success" story, after the SCPA (1984) and before the IPIC Treaty (1989) and TRIPS.

slides.part: Chapter 18: Protection of Semiconductor Integrated Circuit Layout Designs
slides.title: The IPIC Treaty and TRIPS Article 35
slides.html:
The IPIC Treaty, adopted at Washington in 1989, never entered into force, but TRIPS Article 35 makes WTO members apply most of its substantive provisions.

The Treaty on Intellectual Property in Respect of Integrated Circuits (IPIC Treaty) was adopted at Washington in 1989, which is why it is also called the Washington Treaty. It never entered into force.

Its substance survived through TRIPS. Article 35 of TRIPS requires WTO members to protect layout designs in accordance with most of its substantive provisions, with the additions in Articles 36 to 38.

Art. 35, TRIPS. Protection in accordance with Articles 2 to 7 (other than Article 6(3)), 12 and 16(3) of the IPIC Treaty.

  1. IPIC Treaty adopted at Washington in 1989; it never entered into force.
  2. TRIPS Article 35 incorporates IPIC Articles 2 to 7 (other than Article 6(3)), 12 and 16(3).
  3. TRIPS Articles 36 to 38 add their own rules: scope, acts not requiring authorisation, and term.

Exam focus. The duty to protect layout designs comes through TRIPS, not through the IPIC Treaty itself, which never entered into force. Say "IPIC as incorporated by TRIPS Article 35".

slides.part: Chapter 18: Protection of Semiconductor Integrated Circuit Layout Designs
slides.title: TRIPS Articles 36 to 38
slides.html:
TRIPS adds three rules of its own: which acts are unlawful (Art. 36), which acts need no authorisation (Art. 37), and the minimum term (Art. 38).

Read Art. 36 as a chain down the supply line: the layout design, the chip that incorporates it, and the product that incorporates the chip, the last only while it still contains the unlawful copy. Art. 37(1) then protects the innocent buyer in that chain until notice, after which a royalty is payable.

slides.part: Chapter 18: Protection of Semiconductor Integrated Circuit Layout Designs
slides.title: The term: a ten year floor
slides.html:
TRIPS Article 38 sets a floor of at least ten years and lets a member cut protection off fifteen years after the layout was created.

Article 38 sets the term differently depending on whether a member requires registration:

Art. 38(1): registration required

At least ten years from the filing date or the first commercial exploitation anywhere in the world.

Art. 38(2): no registration

At least ten years from first commercial exploitation.

Art. 38(3): optional cap

A member may provide that protection lapses fifteen years after creation of the layout design (the "maximum 15 years").

Why two different starting points? A registration system has a filing date to count from; a system without registration has only the date the design reached the market. The cap in Art. 38(3) runs from creation, so it applies whatever the system.

The national laws in these notes sit on the floor: the SCPA gives ten years, and India's SICLD Act gives ten years (consistent with TRIPS Article 38).

Remember: "Ten at least; a member may cap at fifteen": ten from filing or first commercial exploitation, an optional lapse fifteen years from creation.

slides.part: Chapter 18: Protection of Semiconductor Integrated Circuit Layout Designs
slides.title: The SICLD Act: key definitions
slides.html:
India protects chip layouts under the SICLD Act, 2000; its two key definitions are layout design (s. 2(h)) and semiconductor integrated circuit (s. 2(r)).

India's statute is the Semiconductor Integrated Circuits Layout Design Act, 2000 (SICLD Act): Act No. 37 of 2000 (4 September 2000), administered by the Semiconductor Integrated Circuits Layout Design Registry (SICLDR).

Section 2(h): layout design. A layout of transistors and other circuitry elements, including lead wires connecting such elements, expressed in any manner in a semiconductor integrated circuit.

Section 2(r): semiconductor integrated circuit. A product having transistors and other circuitry elements inseparably formed on or inside a semiconductor or insulating material and designed to perform an electronic circuitry function.

Read the two together: what is protected is the layout, and it must be expressed in a semiconductor integrated circuit as defined in Section 2(r).

Exam focus. A printed circuit board cannot be registered. Quote Section 2(h) word for word in a definition question; it is the first half of practice question 1.

slides.part: Chapter 18: Protection of Semiconductor Integrated Circuit Layout Designs
slides.title: Registrability: Section 7
slides.html:
Section 7(1) bars four kinds of layout design from registration, and Section 7(2) defines the first and most important requirement, originality.

Section 7(1): prohibition of registration. A layout design shall not be registered if it:

  • (a) is not original;
  • (b) has been commercially exploited anywhere in India or in a convention country;
  • (c) is not inherently distinctive; or
  • (d) is not inherently capable of being distinguished from any other registered layout design.

Section 7(2): original. A layout design is original if it results from its creator’s own intellectual efforts and is not commonly known to creators of layout designs and manufacturers of semiconductor integrated circuits at the time of its creation.

Originality has two limbs, and both must be met: the design is the creator's own intellectual efforts (not copied), and it is not commonly known to the trade at the time of creation (not commonplace). This mirrors the EU Directive's test.

Remember: "Only Exceptional Designs Deserve registration": not Original (a), commercially Exploited (b), not Distinctive (c), not Distinguishable (d).

Only a registered layout design can be enforced; Section 18 defines infringement, with exceptions for reverse engineering (s. 18(3)) and written consent (s. 18(7)).

Section 18: infringement. Reproducing a registered layout design, or importing, selling or otherwise distributing for commercial purposes the layout design or a circuit incorporating it.

  1. Section 18(3): analysis exception. A person who creates another original layout design through scientific evaluation or analysis of a registered one may incorporate it. This is India's reverse engineering exception, the counterpart of SCPA Section 906(a).
  2. Section 18(7): consent. Acts done with the registered proprietor’s written consent do not infringe.

slides.part: Quick revision
slides.title: Part E in eight points
slides.html:
Layout designs get sui generis protection because copyright misses function and patents demand an inventive step; the SCPA, the EU, TRIPS and India built it.

Revision summary

  1. A layout design is the three dimensional arrangement of circuit elements in a chip.
  2. It is protected by sui generis laws because copyright does not reach function and patent law demands an inventive step.
  3. The United States led with the SCPA (1984) and its reverse engineering exception (Section 906(a)).
  4. The EU followed with Directive 87/54/EEC.
  5. The IPIC Treaty (1989) never entered into force but is incorporated into TRIPS Articles 35 to 38 (ten year minimum term).
  6. India's Act of 2000 defines layout design (Section 2(h)) and semiconductor integrated circuit (Section 2(r)).
  7. It bars registration of unoriginal, commercially exploited or indistinctive designs (Section 7) and defines infringement in Section 18.
  8. It has been little used.

slides.part: Answer plans
slides.title: Plans: definition, Section 906(a), term
slides.html:
Short answers score by stating the exact provision first, then adding the reason or comparison that shows understanding.

Q1. Define layout design under Section 2(h) of the SICLD Act. Why do copyright and patent law fit layout designs poorly?

  1. Plain meaning first: the three dimensional arrangement of transistors and connections in the chip layers, fixed in masks ("topography"; "mask work" in the US).
  2. Quote Section 2(h): a layout of transistors and other circuitry elements, including lead wires, expressed in any manner in a semiconductor integrated circuit; add Section 2(r), and that a printed circuit board cannot be registered.
  3. Copyright: cannot protect functional aspects, and a circuit arrangement is largely dictated by function.
  4. Patent: cannot protect mere rearrangement; improved arrangements of known elements fail inventive step; Section 3(o) of the Patents Act, 1970 excludes IC topographies.
  5. Conclude: hence a sui generis right (SCPA: patent registration, copyright originality and anti-copying, competition-policy reverse engineering).

Q2. What does Section 906(a) of the SCPA permit, and what is its Indian counterpart?

  1. State Section 906(a): reproduction of a mask work solely for teaching, analysing or evaluating its concepts or techniques.
  2. Second limb: the person may incorporate the results in an original mask work made for distribution.
  3. Explain it as the competition-policy element of the SCPA hybrid.
  4. Indian counterpart: Section 18(3) of the SICLD Act: a person who creates another original layout design through scientific evaluation or analysis of a registered one may incorporate it.
  5. Conclude: both laws leave ideas free to study, but the result must itself be original.

Q3. State the term of protection under TRIPS Article 38.

  1. Art. 38(1): where registration is required, at least ten years from the filing date or the first commercial exploitation anywhere in the world.
  2. Art. 38(2): where it is not required, at least ten years from first commercial exploitation.
  3. Art. 38(3): a member may provide that protection lapses fifteen years after creation (the "maximum 15 years").
  4. Conclude with practice: India and the SCPA both give ten years, consistent with Article 38.

slides.part: Answer plans
slides.title: Plans: the essay and the problem
slides.html:
For the essay, set the laws against how little they are used; for the problem, take each firm separately through Section 18 and its exceptions.

Q4. "Sui generis protection for chip layouts has been a legislative success and a practical failure." Discuss with reference to the SCPA, Directive 87/54/EEC, TRIPS and the Indian Act.

  1. Introduce the layout design and why sui generis protection was needed: copyright does not reach function, patent law demands an inventive step, and Section 3(o) excludes topographies.
  2. Legislative success, in date order: SCPA, 1984 (mask works, ten years, Section 906(a)); Directive 87/54/EEC of 16 December 1986 (own intellectual effort, not commonplace; topography, not the microchip); IPIC Treaty, 1989, never in force but carried into TRIPS by Article 35; TRIPS Articles 36 to 38 (scope, innocent infringement, ten year minimum).
  3. India: SICLD Act, 2000 (Act No. 37 of 2000; SICLDR): Sections 2(h) and 2(r), Section 7, Sections 16 to 19, Section 18(3), ten year term.
  4. Practical failure: the Act has been very little used; reportedly only two layout designs have been registered.
  5. Conclude: the statement is borne out: a full framework at national, regional and international level, but seldom used in India.

Q5. Problem: an Indian start up registers a layout design. A rival buys its chips, analyses them and produces a new chip with a different, original layout performing the same function. A third firm imports chips containing an exact copy of the registered layout. Advise the start up.

  1. Issues: whether either firm infringes under Section 18.
  2. Rules: Sections 7, 17 and 18 (including Section 18(3)); TRIPS Articles 36 and 37; SCPA Section 906(a) for comparison. Note that the design is registered, so Section 16 is no bar.
  3. Application (the rival): its new original layout falls within the analysis exception in Section 18(3); performing the same function is not copying the layout.
  4. Application (the importer): importing chips with an exact copy for commercial purposes infringes, subject to any innocent infringement defence and the royalty rule (TRIPS Article 37).
  5. Conclusion: sue the importer; no claim against the rival unless its layout is in substance a copy.
